profile.summary: This is the benchmark published with EsViritu, a virus taxonomic profiler, not an independent suite. Five profilers (EsViritu, Kraken2, Centrifuger, Metabuli and Sylph) are run over a sweep of their own sensitivity and specificity parameters, all querying the same Virus Pathogen Database, on three sets: synthetic reads from seven real virus genomes 75.9% to 95.6% identical to their closest reference, seven pathogen-free negative control libraries, and six mock communities of mutated virus genomes in a bacterial and human background. It measures what a reader of a metagenomic virus report needs to know: how few reads a tool needs to call a divergent virus, how often it calls something that is not there, and how close the profile is to the true composition.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three properties, each with its own set. Sensitivity to divergence and depth: how often a tool reports the right family from synthetic reads of a genome that sits well below the identity of anything in the database, at 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 reads. Specificity: how many false-positive reads and false species a tool reports on libraries that contain no pathogen. Profile accuracy: how close a tool's community profile is to the known composition of a mock community, by detection and by relative abundance, at every taxonomic rank. The authors' framing is that a profiler must do both halves at once, reporting a virus from a single read without ever reporting one that is absent.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Every tool builds its own index from the same genome sequences and the same NCBI taxonomy dump, which is the design feature that makes the comparison about algorithms rather than reference content. The database is Virus Pathogen Database v3.2.4 with one change: the taxonomic labels were taken only from the NCBI TaxDump of 1 June 2026, erasing the custom subspecies labels the standard version uses, and this modified v3.2.4b is deposited on Zenodo. The positive controls are reads synthesised with bbtools randomreads.sh from seven reference genomes spanning 75.9% to 95.6% identity to their closest database entry. The negative controls are seven pathogen-free libraries: human genome mock reads, mouse RNA, anaerobic digester, freshwater, marine water, hot springs and soil. The mock communities are six sets, three of 90 genomes drawn at random from the database and three of 60 genomes with at most one assembly per family, each mutated to a ladder of 80, 85, 90, 95, 98 and 100% identity, with 10,000 viral read pairs in total per community and a background of 100 random bacterial genomes plus the human genome at 50,000,000 reads (50,010,000 reads per community).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities, Virus Pathogen Database. Zenodo record: files and licence

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each tool is run over a grid of the parameters that govern its sensitivity and specificity, and a single headline setting is then chosen per tool as the one that maximises specificity while keeping as much sensitivity as possible. Detection in the positive controls is modelled by Firth-penalised logistic regression of detection on tool, depth and genome, with EsViritu as the reference level and Benjamini-Hochberg correction on the tool contrasts, chosen because the most and least sensitive tools separate completely; each genome is summarised by its LD50, the depth at which detection reaches 50%. The negative controls are compared with Friedman tests, post-hoc Wilcoxon tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and Kendall's W effect sizes. Mock community profiles are scored at every rank for F1, Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and correlation, with abundance calibration by Lin's concordance correlation coefficient in a pooled and a resolvable stratum, and under two definitions of ground truth: strict provenance lineage, and divergence-capped, which caps the rank a tool can be credited with by the genome's identity to its reference.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities; Results

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: On the positive controls Metabuli was the most sensitive tool, reaching 50% detection at or near a single read for most genomes and detecting more often than EsViritu (odds ratio 127.6, p = 0.012); EsViritu held single-read sensitivity down to 85.05% identity, Kraken2 and Centrifuger at their headline settings detected nothing below 85% identity and reached single-read sensitivity only at 95%, and Sylph failed to reach 50% detection in six of the seven genomes at any depth. The negative controls reverse the order: EsViritu in short-read mode and Sylph at all parameters were effectively clean, each with a median of zero false species and EsViritu with one spurious call in total, while the settings that made the other tools competitive on sensitivity produced very high false-positive counts, Centrifuger going from near zero to hundreds of thousands of false hits per library depending on one parameter. On the mock communities the paper reports EsViritu as better than or equal to every other tool on virtually all communities, ranks and metrics, under both ground-truth definitions. The headline settings chosen were EsViritu sr, Centrifuger minimum hit length 100 with minimum score 0, Kraken2 confidence 0.5 with minimum hit group 2, Metabuli precision 1 with minimum score 0.15, and Sylph 10 k-mers per genome.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The benchmark's own inputs and results are deposited on Zenodo, including the modified database and the positive, negative and mock result archives, and the processing and analysis repository is released with a stable tag. The tool under test installs from Bioconda in two commands, needs its database downloaded from Zenodo (about 400 MB decompressed, with a published md5), and is run per sample with a reads file, a sample name and an output directory. Reproducing the comparison itself needs the other four tools built against the same database, which the paper describes but the sources read do not give as commands.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Three sets, all synthetic or pathogen-free. Positive controls: synthetic read sets from seven real virus genomes at 75.9% to 95.6% identity to their closest database reference, at four depths with ten permutations each. Negative controls: seven pathogen-free libraries (human genome mock reads, mouse RNA, anaerobic digester, freshwater, marine water, hot springs, soil). Mock communities: six communities, three of 90 genomes and three of 60 genomes, each at 50,010,000 total reads. The shared reference is Virus Pathogen Database v3.2.4b, built from 63 virus families and described elsewhere in the paper as nearly 20,000 genomes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities, Virus Pathogen Database; Discussion

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: There is no train and test split: none of the tools is trained here, and each is run on every sample. The structure is by experiment and by condition: read depth (1, 10, 100, 1,000) with ten permutations for the positive controls, background type for the negative controls, and the identity ladder (80, 85, 90, 95, 98, 100%) and community design (90 random genomes or 60 one-per-family) for the mock communities. Two ground-truth definitions are applied to the mock communities. The paper is inconsistent on where the divergence-capped metrics apply: the Methods say only the one-per-family communities were measured with them, while the Results say both strict and divergence-capped metrics are reported for all six communities in Fig. S2.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls and Mock communities; Results

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Per experiment. Positive controls: detection probability, higher better, and LD50, the depth giving 50% detection, lower better. Negative controls: false-positive read percentage and false species counts, lower better. Mock communities: F1 with precision and recall for detection, higher better, and Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, lower better, with Pearson and Spearman correlation to ground truth and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient for abundance calibration, all computed at every taxonomic rank.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities; Figure 3 caption; Results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Four other profilers at pinned versions: Kraken2 v2.17.1, Centrifuger v1.1.1-r309, Metabuli v1.2.0 and Sylph v0.9.0, each run across a sweep of its own thresholds, for example Kraken2's confidence score from 0 to 0.5 and minimum hit group from 2 to 5. EsViritu v1.3.1 is the tool under test and was run in both its short-read sr and sensitive sense configurations.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters; Results

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The controls here are about reference content and divergence rather than training data. All five tools index the same genomes and the same taxonomy dump, so none has a richer reference than another; the custom subspecies labels were stripped so that no tool is credited or penalised for labels only one database version carries; the positive control genomes are deliberately 75.9% to 95.6% identical to anything in the database; and the mock community genomes are mutated away from their references on a ladder down to 80%. The divergence-capped ground truth caps the rank a tool may be credited with at a given identity, which stops a tool scoring for a species call it cannot support.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters, Positive controls, Mock communities; Results

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Replication and formal tests, but not intervals on most headline numbers. Ten independent permutations per genome and depth in the positive controls, feeding a Firth-penalised logistic regression with Benjamini-Hochberg corrected tool contrasts and reported odds ratios with p values; Friedman tests with post-hoc Wilcoxon tests, Benjamini-Hochberg correction and Kendall's W for the negative controls; six independent communities for the mock analysis, with results reported under both ground-truth definitions as a robustness check. Divergence is treated descriptively because it is confounded with genome, one genome per identity level.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities; Results

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: Depends on the experiment. Positive controls: one synthetic read set from one genome at one depth, scored as detected or not when the tool reports the corresponding family. Negative controls: one pathogen-free sequencing library, scored by the false-positive reads and false species in it. Mock communities: one community profile, compared with the known composition at each taxonomic rank.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Viruses of humans, animals and plants as the targets, drawn from the 63 families in the Virus Pathogen Database. The backgrounds are host and environmental: human, mouse, 100 random bacterial genomes, and environmental metagenomes from an anaerobic digester, freshwater, marine water, hot springs and soil. The database itself was screened against human, dog, mouse, cow, macaque, chicken, cat and rat genomes to mask host-derived regions.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Virus Pathogen Database, Negative controls, Mock communities

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None in the wet-lab sense for the benchmark itself: the positive controls and mock communities are simulated reads, generated with bbtools randomreads.sh and with InSilicoSeq using log-normal abundance distributions and a NovaSeq error model. The negative controls are real sequencing libraries, but from pathogen-free host, synthetic and environmental material rather than from a clinical specimen with a reference test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Sequencing reads and the shared reference database, nothing else. Each tool builds its index from the same FASTA and taxonomy dump and is given the read set; EsViritu takes a FASTQ (gzipped allowed), a sample name and an output directory, with paired, unpaired or interleaved input.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters. Repository: README.md, Running the tool

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: No training. Each tool is a reference-based classifier run at fixed parameter settings; the only tuning is the published parameter sweep, from which one headline setting per tool is chosen to maximise specificity while keeping as much sensitivity as possible. The sweep and the headline choice are made on the same benchmark data.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters; Results

strengths.text: The reference set is held constant. All five tools build their index from the same genomes and the same taxonomy dump, and the subspecies labels unique to one database version were removed so no tool is scored on labels another cannot see.

Each tool is swept across its own sensitivity and specificity parameters rather than run at one setting, which is what exposes that the settings making a tool competitive on detection are the ones that flood the negative controls.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters; Results

strengths.text: Sensitivity and specificity are tested on separate purpose-built sets, with replication and formal statistics: ten permutations per genome and depth with a regression that handles complete separation, and Friedman with post-hoc Wilcoxon tests on the negative controls.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls and Negative controls

strengths.text: Two ground-truth definitions are reported rather than one. The divergence-capped truth refuses credit for a species call on a genome too divergent to support it, and results under the strict definition are reported alongside as a robustness check.

limitations.text: The benchmark was built and run by the developers of the tool it favours, and EsViritu's own database is the shared reference, so the comparison is on home ground even though the content is identical for all tools.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Tools and parameters; Code and data availability

limitations.text: No clinical specimen is involved. Every positive signal is simulated and every negative is a pathogen-free library, so the benchmark says nothing about agreement with a reference diagnostic test on real patient samples.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

limitations.text: The positive control panel is seven genomes, one per identity level, and the paper says identity is therefore confounded with genome and treats divergence descriptively. The headline parameter settings are also chosen on the same data they are then reported on.

One comparison is not like for like: Sylph reports a k-mer containment sequence abundance that the authors say was not readily comparable to the other abundance metrics, so its abundance results are not on the same footing.

The article is a preprint record under a non-commercial licence, and most per-tool numbers live in supplementary tables rather than the text, so the figures a reader can quote from the article itself are limited.

profile.summary: This is the evaluation published with Talos, an open-source tool that automates variant prioritisation for rare disease reanalysis. It is not a reusable suite: the reference is the set of diagnoses already known in two cohorts, 401 Acute Care Genomics probands and 688 Rare Genomes Project families, each reprocessed through one standardised calling pipeline. The measures are how many known diagnoses Talos returns and how many candidate variants a human must read to find them, reported separately for trios, singletons and the whole cohort and under default and strict filtering. A paired comparison against Exomiser and a prospective deployment on 4,735 undiagnosed individuals are reported alongside.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Assessing Talos performance; Table 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two quantities in tension. Sensitivity: of the diagnoses already known in a cohort, how many does the tool put in front of an analyst. Workload: how many candidate variants the analyst has to read, per proband and per diagnosis. The cohorts were chosen so that the tool could be measured against manual analysis and with and without parental data, which is why every figure is reported separately for trios, singletons and the full cohort. The design question behind it is whether automated reanalysis can be run often enough to be sustainable, which is why the burden per case matters as much as the recall.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Assessing Talos performance; Table 1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Both cohorts were reprocessed from raw sequencing data through one pipeline, GATK for short variants, GATK-SV for structural variants in genomes and GATK-gCNV for copy number variants in exomes, and Talos was evaluated against the variants that pipeline detected. That matters for the denominator: of 208 known diagnoses in the ACG trios, 196 (94%) were detectable by the pipeline, and of 57 in the RGP trios, 54 (95%) were. The ACG cohort is 401 critically ill infants and children given ultra-rapid clinical genomic testing in Australia between 2018 and 2022, 115 exomes and 286 genomes, 94% trios, with a prior manual diagnostic yield of 55%. The RGP cohort is 688 families recruited remotely across the United States and sequenced at the Broad Institute before September 2022, 298 singletons and 390 trios, prior yield 15.4%, median proband age 26 years.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Assessing Talos performance, Acute Care Genomics cohort, Rare Genomes Project cohort; Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Talos is run on the reprocessed call sets and its returned candidates are compared with the known diagnoses. Two filtering settings are reported: default, and strict, which requires a phenotype match. Each cell of Table 1 gives the diagnoses found with the percentage of detectable diagnoses, the total candidate variants, candidates per proband and candidates per diagnosis. Success for Talos is simply that the causative variant is returned under default settings, since Talos returns an unranked set rather than a ranking. Against Exomiser, success is defined by rank position (top 1, top 5, top 10, or unconstrained), and because the two tools run on the same families the comparison uses McNemar's exact test on the discordant pairs with two-sided p values. The tool is described as deterministic and automated, so its output does not depend on the investigator, although prior diagnoses were known at evaluation time.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Exomiser comparison and Statistics and reproducibility

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: In the ACG trios Talos returned 177 of the 196 detectable diagnoses (90%) from 487 candidate variants, 1.3 per proband and 2.8 per diagnosis; across the full ACG cohort 186 of 208 (89%) from 523 candidates. Singletons cost more per diagnosis: 170 of 208 (82%) from 729 candidates, 4.3 per diagnosis. In the RGP cohort the trios gave 47 of 54 (87%) at 1.3 candidates per proband but 11.0 candidates per diagnosis, and the full cohort 80 of 93 (86%) at 13.7 per diagnosis. Strict filtering lowers both: for example 164 of 196 (83%) in ACG trios at 2.5 candidates per diagnosis. Against Exomiser on 194 ACG trio families with SNV or indel diagnoses, Exomiser found 172 (89%) with all variants considered, 164 (85%) in its top 10, 157 (81%) in its top five and 127 (65%) at rank one; McNemar's test found no difference at all-variants or top 10 and favoured Talos at top five and top one. In the prospective cohort of 4,735 undiagnosed individuals, Talos output led to 241 new diagnoses in 238 individuals, a 5.1% additional yield, all later classified pathogenic or likely pathogenic by accredited laboratories; across 29 monthly cycles, 92% of those diagnoses came in a cohort's first cycle and later cycles returned an average of five new candidate variants per 1,000 cases.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Results, Acute Care Genomics cohort, Rare Genomes Project cohort, Comparison with other tools, Iterative reanalysis in research and clinical datasets

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Talos is a Nextflow workflow with its dependencies in Docker, run locally or on a cluster. Build the image, download the external annotation resources into a large_files directory, run the preparation workflow that formats ClinVar, PanelApp and AlphaMissense into Hail tables, then run the combined annotation and analysis workflow from a single input TSV naming the cohort, its VCF, the data type, a pedigree and a config file. The annotation workflow is run once per dataset and only the prioritisation workflow is rerun for later reanalysis. Output is a JSON of candidate variants per proband with variant-level and gene-level evidence, inheritance checks and phenotype match tags, plus optional HTML reports and a simplified TSV.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two evaluation cohorts and one prospective deployment. ACG: 401 probands, 208 known diagnoses in the full cohort and 377 trios. RGP: 688 families (298 singletons, 390 trios), 93 known diagnoses in the full cohort, 106 prior diagnoses in the cohort overall. Prospective: 4,735 undiagnosed or partially diagnosed individuals, 3,739 exomes and 996 genomes, of whom 3,737 were analysed as singletons. The abstract describes the validation as 1,089 individuals, which is the 401 plus 688.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train and test split: Talos is a rule and evidence pipeline, not a trained model, so every case in a cohort is analysed. The reported partitions are by family structure (trio only, singleton, full cohort) within each cohort, and by filtering setting (default or strict with phenotype matching). The denominator for sensitivity is the diagnoses detectable by the standardised calling pipeline, not all prior diagnoses.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1 and its footnote; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Diagnoses recovered, as a count and a percentage of the detectable known diagnoses, higher better; and review burden as candidate variants in total, per proband and per diagnosis, lower better. For the prospective cohort the measure is additional diagnostic yield as a percentage of individuals. The Exomiser comparison adds rank-budget recall at top 1, top 5, top 10 and unconstrained, with McNemar's exact test p values on the discordant pairs.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Exomiser comparison; Results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Two kinds. The manual clinical and research analysis that produced the known diagnoses in each cohort is the reference standard. Exomiser v.14 in its default configuration is the one competing tool, run on the same ACG trio SNV and indel call sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Comparison with other tools; Methods, Exomiser comparison

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Weak, and the paper says so plainly: the investigators were not blinded and the prior diagnoses were known at evaluation time, which was necessary to benchmark against manual analysis. The protections are that Talos is deterministic and produces its output without investigator input, that both cohorts were reprocessed through one standardised pipeline so the tool is measured against a fixed call set, and that Exomiser ran on the same families. There is no held-out cohort and no prespecified threshold.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Statistics and reproducibility; Results, Assessing Talos performance

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Little. Counts and percentages are reported without confidence intervals, and no statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. The only inferential statistics are the McNemar exact test p values for the paired Talos against Exomiser comparison at each rank budget. Reproducibility rests on the pipeline being deterministic and on versioning the external annotation sources at run time, which the authors say allows exact reproduction of a given reanalysis cycle.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Statistics and reproducibility and Exomiser comparison

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A case: one proband, with or without parents, and the variant calls for that family. Success or failure is per family (did the known causative variant come back), and the burden measures count candidate variants per proband and per diagnosis.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human. All three cohorts are people with rare disease: critically ill infants and children in Australia, families recruited across the United States and Puerto Rico, and patients referred for genomic testing in Australia.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Clinical exome and genome sequencing, reprocessed from raw data with GATK for short variants, GATK-SV for structural variants and GATK-gCNV for copy number variants. The labels are not assay readouts but clinical diagnoses: the variants previously reported for each case, and for the prospective cohort, variants later classified pathogenic or likely pathogenic by accredited laboratories and submitted to ClinVar.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Assessing Talos performance and Iterative reanalysis; Data availability

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Variant calls and family and phenotype metadata, not sequence. Mandatory: SNV and indel calls as single-sample or multi-sample VCF, a pedigree in PED format and a TOML configuration. Optional: structural and copy number variant calls, Human Phenotype Ontology terms per individual, and a previous results JSON to keep first-seen dates. The paper asks that input variants not be prefiltered beyond standard quality control so that Talos's own filtering applies consistently. Talos also draws on external resources: PanelApp Australia, ClinVar through ClinvArbitration, gnomAD and AlphaMissense.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Talos input requirements; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility. Repository: README.md, inputs and annotation resources

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: None of the machine learning kind. Talos applies logic modules, inheritance-aware filtering, allele frequency filtering and phenotype matching against versioned external evidence; nothing is trained on these cohorts. The only setting varied in the evaluation is default against strict filtering, and Exomiser was run at its default configuration.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Table 1; Methods, Exomiser comparison

strengths.text: Sensitivity and review burden are reported together, per family structure and per filtering setting, so the cost of each gain is visible: the ACG trios return 90% of detectable diagnoses at 1.3 candidates per proband, while RGP singletons return 87% at 18.4 candidates per diagnosis.

The denominator is honest about what the calling pipeline can see. Diagnoses due to variant classes the pipeline does not capture reliably, such as repeat expansions and low-level mosaics, are kept in the cohort and reported as missed, and the detectable subset is stated (196 of 208 in ACG trios, 54 of 57 in RGP trios).
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Acute Care Genomics cohort and Rare Genomes Project cohort; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility

strengths.text: The comparison with Exomiser is paired and analysed as such, with McNemar's exact test on discordant families and a stated reason why unpaired tests would be wrong, and it is reported at several review budgets rather than at one flattering cut.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Exomiser comparison; Results, Comparison with other tools

strengths.text: The tool is open source, containerised and reproducible by design: Docker and Nextflow with the study's configuration files published, and the external evidence sources versioned at run time.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Statistics and reproducibility; Code availability. Repository: README.md, Quick Start

limitations.text: The evaluation was run by the tool's own developers on cohorts whose diagnoses were already known, without blinding or randomisation, so the recall figures are not an independent prospective estimate.

No uncertainty is attached to the headline numbers. Every diagnosis count, percentage and candidates-per-case figure in Table 1 is a point estimate with no interval, and the only p values in the study are for the Exomiser comparison.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility

limitations.text: The cohorts cannot be downloaded openly, so a third party can rerun the benchmark only after gaining controlled access. The RGP data are under controlled access via dbGaP (phs003047). The Australian Genomics data, including genome and exome sequencing data, are available for ethically approved secondary health and medical research use, subject to participant consent, on application to the cohort's data access committee with evidence of ethics approval. What is public without application is the tool and its configuration.

Results depend on moving evidence sources and on local gene panels. Candidates during iterative reanalysis are returned only when the supporting evidence has changed, and the annotation sources are PanelApp Australia, ClinVar and gnomAD at whatever version was current, so a reanalysis elsewhere or later will not give the same output.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Iterative reanalysis; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility

limitations.text: The article itself is under a non-commercial, no-derivatives licence, so the text and tables cannot be redistributed or adapted freely, although the code is MIT.

profile.summary: Gene-MTEB asks how useful a model's frozen sequence embeddings are on metagenomic data. It was introduced with METAGENE-1 as a genomics version of MTEB: eight classification tasks scored by accuracy and eight clustering tasks scored by V-measure, built from Human Microbiome Project sequences, human virus reference sequences and held-out parts of the METAGENE-1 pretraining corpus. A model is used only as an encoder, so it suits someone choosing a frozen genomic encoder for a lightweight downstream model.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3 and Table 3. README.md: introduction and Quick Tour

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The quality of representations a model produces without being trained for the task. The authors say such representations matter for building light predictive models on a frozen foundation model, for interpretability work with sparse autoencoders and for anomaly detection. The classification tasks ask whether an embedding separates labels carried by the sample: which human-infecting virus a read comes from, and the disease status, sex and body source behind an HMP sample. The clustering tasks ask whether embeddings of reference sequences group by taxonomy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. Task metadata in HumanVirusClassification.py, HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassification.py and HumanVirusReferenceClustering.py

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The paper names eight classification tasks (Human-Virus-1 to 4, HMPD-single, HMPD-disease, HMPD-source, HMPD-sex) and eight clustering tasks (HVR and HMPR, each as p2p, s2s-align, s2s-small and s2s-tiny). The data come from the Human Microbiome Project and from held-out portions of the authors' own metagenomic dataset, and the paper points to the project Hugging Face page for access. In the code each task loads one of four Hugging Face dataset repositories at revision main: HumanVirusInfecting, HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstration, HumanVirusReference and HumanMicrobiomeProjectReference. Clustering tasks rename a sequence column to sentences and a taxonomy column to labels, then drop the top taxonomic level as trivial. Every task's metadata records its licence as not specified.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. Task files: dataset blocks, dataset_transform and metadata

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model is used as an encoder only. The paper takes embeddings for all models by mean pooling the last hidden state, fits logistic regression on top of the embeddings for every classification task and runs mini-batch k-means for every clustering task, reporting accuracy and V-measure. The code confirms the rest: each classification task sets its method to logReg, makes one shuffled, unstratified split of the loaded train set whose training fraction is 8 divided by the count of the rarest label, so the rarest label gets about 8 training examples and commoner labels get proportionally more (the code comment says 8 samples per label), with everything else as the test split, and evaluates on test with accuracy as the main score. The clustering tasks evaluate on test with V-measure as the main score, hold the clustering to a maximum label depth of 5, and cap how many documents are embedded, which is what separates the p2p, align, small and tiny variants of the same dataset. All splitting is seeded at 42.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. Task files: __init__, load_data, metadata main_score, class attributes

sections.title: Classification tasks
sections.body: Seven of the eight sit in two files: four Human-Virus tasks, each loading a different configuration (class-1 and its siblings) of the HumanVirusInfecting dataset, and three HMP demonstration tasks for disease, sex and source. All seven are single-sentence tasks scored by accuracy on a test split from one random split whose training fraction is 8 divided by the count of the rarest label. The repository also adds one multi-label classification task on the HMP demonstration sequences, which was not read for this page; the paper's eighth classification row is HMPD-single, printed in the paper as MHPD-single.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Quick Tour. HumanVirusClassification.py and HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassification.py: class definitions. Paper: Section 5.3 and Table 3

sections.title: Clustering tasks
sections.body: Eight tasks, four on human virus reference sequences and four on HMP reference sequences. Each clustering task splits its data with test_size 0.9 (p2p) or 0.995 (align, small, tiny), seed 42, evaluates on the test split only, and caps the number of documents embedded at the variant's max_document_to_embed. The variants differ in how many documents may be embedded: for the virus reference set 40 (p2p), 147 (align, the size of the train split), 40 (small) and 3 (tiny); for the HMP reference set 27, 2198, 27 and 3. The tiny limit of 3 is described in the code as simulating the 3-mer in DNA sequence processing.
sections.source_locator: HumanVirusReferenceClustering.py and HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClustering.py: class attributes and load_data

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: Table 3 of the METAGENE-1 paper compares five models: DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, NT-2.5b-Multi, NT-2.5b-1000g and METAGENE-1. METAGENE-1 has the highest global average, 0.590 against 0.545 for the next model, and the paper singles out the Human-Virus group, where its average of 0.775 is more than 6 points above the others. The spread is not uniform: on HVR-p2p METAGENE-1 scores 0.466 while NT-2.5b-1000g scores 0.650, and both METAGENE-1 and NT-2.5b-Multi reach 1.000 on HVR-s2s-tiny.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 3 and Section 5.3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install the repository's fork of MTEB, wrap your model in an encode method that returns one vector per sequence, and run the sixteen named tasks through the MTEB runner. The repository's own example wraps METAGENE-1 with a Hugging Face AutoModel, tokenises with padding and truncation to 512 tokens, takes the mean of the last hidden state over tokens, fixes the seed at 42, and passes the list of sixteen task names to mteb.get_tasks before calling evaluation.run.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation; Example Using METAGENE-1

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Sixteen tasks over four Hugging Face dataset repositories: HumanVirusInfecting (four classification tasks), HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstration (three classification tasks plus one multi-label task), HumanVirusReference (four clustering tasks) and HumanMicrobiomeProjectReference (four clustering tasks). The paper gives no row or sequence counts for any task, and the files read print only the per-task document limits, not dataset sizes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. README.md: Quick Tour. Task files: dataset blocks

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Each task cuts its own test split from a single loaded train set, with the seed fixed at 42. Classification: one shuffled, unstratified split with training fraction 8/M, where M is the count of the rarest label, so the rarest label gets about 8 training examples and commoner labels more; the rest becomes the test split. Clustering: the p2p tasks use test_size 0.9 and the align, small and tiny tasks use test_size 0.995. Every task evaluates on the test split only.
facts.source_locator: Task files: load_data and metadata eval_splits

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Accuracy for the classification tasks and V-measure for the clustering tasks, higher better in both cases; the task metadata names accuracy and v_measure as each task's main score. Table 3 also prints a mean per group (Human-Virus, HMPD, HVR, HMPR) and a global average, but the paper does not say how the global average is weighted.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3 and Table 3. Task metadata main_score

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Four other models alongside METAGENE-1: DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, NT-2.5b-Multi and NT-2.5b-1000g.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: One is described and it is weak: the paper says the task data come from the Human Microbiome Project and from held-out portions of its own metagenomic dataset. No sequence identity cut-off, time split or held-out taxonomic group is described, and the baselines' own pretraining corpora are not discussed in this context.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None is reported: Table 3 prints one value per model and task with no interval or replicate. The code fixes the seed at 42 before loading and splitting each task, so a repeated run uses the same split rather than giving a spread.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a nucleotide sequence. In the classification tasks it carries a sample-level label; in the clustering tasks the sequence column is renamed to sentences and its taxonomy becomes the label list.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human-associated: viruses that infect a human host, human virus reference sequences, and bacterial and other sequences from human microbiome samples. The tasks' metadata records the domain as Medical, and the task descriptions name the human host.
facts.source_locator: README.md: introduction. Task metadata: description and domains

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. The labels are not experimental measurements: they are metagenomic sequencing samples with metadata (disease status, sex, body source, virus of origin) or reference sequences with a taxonomy, and each task's metadata records its annotations as derived.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Sequence only. A model is called as an encoder over a list of sequences and must return one vector each; the paper takes every model's embedding by mean pooling the last hidden state, and the repository's example truncates to 512 tokens.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. README.md: Example Using METAGENE-1

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Frozen embeddings only. The paper calls this a zero-shot assessment of representations: the model is not fine-tuned, and the only fitting is the logistic regression trained on a small split for the classification tasks (training fraction 8 divided by the count of the rarest label), with mini-batch k-means for the clustering tasks.

strengths.text: The tasks are released as code in a fork of MTEB, with each task's dataset, split rule, evaluation split and main score written in its metadata, so the protocol can be read rather than inferred, and the repository's example lists the sixteen task names needed to reproduce the table.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Example Using METAGENE-1. HumanVirusClassification.py: TaskMetadata

strengths.text: All models are embedded the same way, by mean pooling the last hidden state, so the comparison does not mix pooling conventions.

Both classification and clustering are included, and the clustering variants vary the number of documents embedded within the same dataset, which exposes how a model behaves at different amounts of context.

limitations.text: The benchmark was introduced by the authors of one of the models compared on it, and in the paper METAGENE-1 has the best global average. Part of the task data is drawn from held-out portions of METAGENE-1's own metagenomic dataset.

Several tasks are very small. The clustering tasks embed at most 40 documents (virus reference) or 27 (HMP reference) in their p2p and small variants and only 3 in their tiny variants, and the classification tasks fit on a split sized to give about 8 examples of the rarest label. Two models already score 1.000 on HVR-s2s-tiny.
limitations.source_locator: Task files: class attributes and load_data. Paper: Table 3

limitations.text: No per-task uncertainty is published, and because each task splits its data once under a fixed seed, repeating a run does not produce a spread to compare small differences against.

The data terms are unstated. Every task's metadata records its licence as not specified, and the dataset repositories are pinned only to the moving revision main, so a later run may not use the same data.

steps.title: Run the sixteen tasks with a model wrapper
steps.shell:
cat > run_gene_mteb.py <<'PY'
import mteb
from mteb.encoder_interface import PromptType
import numpy as np
from tqdm import tqdm
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer
from transformers.trainer_utils import set_seed
import torch


class LlamaWrapper:
    def __init__(self, model_name, seed, max_length=512):
        self.seed = seed
        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
        self.model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
            model_name,
            torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
            trust_remote_code=True,
            device_map="cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "auto")
        self.model.config.pad_token_id = self.tokenizer.pad_token_id
        self.max_length = max_length
        self.model.eval()

    def encode(self, sentences, task_name=None, prompt_type=None, **kwargs):
        set_seed(self.seed)
        batch_size = kwargs.get("batch_size", 32)
        embeddings = []
        for i in tqdm(range(0, len(sentences), batch_size)):
            batch = sentences[i:i + batch_size]
            inputs = self.tokenizer(
                batch, padding=True, truncation=True,
                max_length=self.max_length, return_tensors="pt").to(self.model.device)
            if "token_type_ids" in inputs:
                del inputs["token_type_ids"]
            with torch.no_grad():
                outputs = self.model(**inputs)
                batch_embeddings = outputs.last_hidden_state.mean(dim=1)
            embeddings.extend(batch_embeddings.cpu().to(torch.float32).numpy())
        return np.array(embeddings)


model = LlamaWrapper(model_name="metagene-ai/METAGENE-1", seed=42)
tasks = mteb.get_tasks(tasks=[
    "HumanVirusClassificationOne",
    "HumanVirusClassificationTwo",
    "HumanVirusClassificationThree",
    "HumanVirusClassificationFour",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassificationDisease",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassificationSex",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassificationSource",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationMultiLabelClassification",
    "HumanVirusReferenceClusteringP2P",
    "HumanVirusReferenceClusteringS2SAlign",
    "HumanVirusReferenceClusteringS2SSmall",
    "HumanVirusReferenceClusteringS2STiny",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClusteringP2P",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClusteringS2SAlign",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClusteringS2SSmall",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClusteringS2STiny",
])
evaluation = mteb.MTEB(tasks=tasks)

PY

profile.summary: These are the variant effect prediction benchmarks the GPN-Star authors assembled to evaluate their alignment- and phylogeny-aware genomic language model. Seven classification tasks pit curated pathogenic or causal variants against common or non-causal controls (ClinVar and COSMIC missense, OMIM and HGMD non-coding, UK Biobank fine-mapped coding and non-coding, and promoter variants), scored by area under the precision-recall curve; a deep mutational scanning task reports Spearman correlation on 31 human protein assays; and two further tasks measure gnomAD rare versus common enrichment and gene discovery in rare variant association testing. The benchmark datasets are published on Hugging Face, so the comparison is reusable even though the paper's own role was to show one model.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a genome-wide score separates variants that matter from variants that do not, across the settings where that question is asked in practice. Coding: pathogenic against benign missense in ClinVar, cancer-frequent against population-common missense in COSMIC, and fitness measured by deep mutational scanning. Non-coding: curated pathogenic regulatory variants from OMIM and HGMD against common controls, and fine-mapped GWAS variants with high against low posterior inclusion probability. Then two uses rather than classifications: whether the score's deleterious tail is enriched for rare gnomAD variants, and whether adding the score as an annotation finds more genes in rare variant association testing.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each task reuses a published resource at a stated version and, for the non-coding tasks, a matched control design taken from TraitGym. ClinVar is release 20220924, pathogenic against benign missense. COSMIC frequent mutations are those in more than 0.1% of whole-genome or whole-exome samples in MutantCensus v98, against gnomAD common missense. ProteinGym contributes 31 human protein assays from v0.1, restricted to amino acid substitutions reachable by a single nucleotide change, taking the most deleterious such change by CADD. For OMIM and HGMD, each pathogenic variant is matched with nine control variants on chromosome, molecular consequence and distance to the transcription start site; for fine-mapped non-coding variants the matching adds LD score and minor allele frequency, while for fine-mapped coding variants only allele frequency is matched. The gnomAD task uses v3.1.2 allele frequencies and follows the GPN-MSA protocol: the deleterious tail is cut at the threshold giving 30 false discoveries and rare variants are subsampled to the number of common variants in each consequence category.
sections.source_locator: Supplementary Information: Evaluation Benchmarks, Datasets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: AUPRC on the complete benchmark set, with 95% confidence intervals from 1,000 class-stratified bootstrap resamples, for the seven classification tasks; Spearman correlation per assay for ProteinGym, shown as a distribution over the 31 assays. One rule keeps the comparison fair across many models: for each benchmark only variants for which every compared model has a prediction are used. The rare variant association testing experiment runs DeepRVAT on 34 UK Biobank quantitative traits using whole-exome data from 161,822 unrelated individuals of European ancestry, keeping variants below 0.1% minor allele frequency, with and without the three GPN-Star scores as added annotations, repeated three times with different random seeds; the outcome is the number of significant genes at family-wise error rate below 0.05 and how many of those replicate in larger published studies.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 2 caption; Results, Rare variant association testing. Supplementary Information: Evaluation Benchmarks

sections.title: The models compared
sections.body: The comparison set is unusually wide and is pinned in the supplementary methods: classical conservation scores PhyloP and PhastCons at three evolutionary timescales, the ensemble CADD v1.7 raw scores, single-sequence genomic language models Nucleotide Transformer 2.5B multispecies and Evo 2 at 7B and 40B with an 8,192 base pair context, the earlier alignment model GPN-MSA, protein language models ESM-1b, ESM-2 and ESM-3-open, the sequence-to-function models Enformer, Borzoi and AlphaGenome, the allele-frequency-informed AlphaMissense and PrimateAI-3D, the promoter-specific PromoterAI, SpeciesLM and GPN-Promoter, and Roulette mutation rate estimates. Most scores were taken precomputed from the original authors or from TraitGym rather than recomputed.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Extended Data Fig. 1 caption. Supplementary Information: Compared models

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: The paper reports GPN-Star first on every benchmark. On ClinVar missense, GPN-Star (V) has the highest AUPRC, matching ESM-1b and beating ESM-2 and ESM-3-open. On OMIM and HGMD non-coding variants GPN-Star (M) is best, and the sequence-to-function models do substantially worse than alignment-based and phylogenetic models. On fine-mapped coding variants GPN-Star (M) leads, with AlphaMissense and PrimateAI-3D substantially outperformed despite their use of allele frequency; on fine-mapped non-coding variants it leads again, with Evo 2 of limited value. On promoter variants it beats the promoter-specific models by a wide margin. Adding all three GPN-Star scores to DeepRVAT raised the significant gene count from 383 to 402 on average and the replicating subset from 338 to 353. No cross-model score is printed in text form; the AUPRC values for competing models are only in Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 1. For reference, the ablation table in the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Table 3), which compares GPN-Star architecture variants trained the same way rather than competing models, gives the default GPN-Star architecture (mean of three initialisations) 0.896 on ClinVar, 0.391 on COSMIC, 0.383 on ProteinGym, 0.239 on fine-mapped coding, 0.713 on OMIM, 0.222 on fine-mapped non-coding and 0.570 on HGMD.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The benchmark datasets, the pretrained models and the whole-genome alignments are published in one Hugging Face collection, and precomputed GPN-Star scores for every possible single nucleotide variant in the human genome and five model organisms are released separately. The code to train, run inference and reproduce the main analyses is on GitHub with a Zenodo archive. To score a new model on these benchmarks a user needs the dataset repositories from the collection, for example clinvar_vs_benign, cosmic, omim_traitgym, ukb_finemapped_coding, ukb_finemapped_nc_traitgym and gnomad_balanced, and should apply the paper's rule of keeping only variants that every compared model can score.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Ten tasks over eight sources: ClinVar release 20220924 (pathogenic against benign missense), COSMIC MutantCensus v98 against gnomAD v3 common missense, ProteinGym v0.1 restricted to 31 human protein assays, OMIM and HGMD curated pathogenic regulatory variants against gnomAD common controls at nine controls per positive, UK Biobank fine-mapped variants across 65 traits (coding) and 83 traits (non-coding), promoter subsets of the OMIM and fine-mapped sets, gnomAD v3.1.2 allele frequencies, and UK Biobank whole-exome data for 34 quantitative traits. The variant counts per benchmark are printed only in the figure panel headings, which are images, so no count is recorded here.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two different things are split here. The benchmarks themselves are evaluated whole, with no train and test division, because the scores are zero-shot; the structure comes from the matched control design (nine controls per positive for OMIM, HGMD and fine-mapped non-coding, matched on chromosome, consequence and distance to the transcription start site, plus LD score and allele frequency for the latter, and allele frequency only for fine-mapped coding). The model's own training split keeps chromosomes 1 to 20, X and Y for training, chromosome 21 for validation and chromosome 22 as the held-out test chromosome, which is the chromosome used for the gnomAD allele frequency analyses.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUPRC for the seven classification benchmarks, higher better, computed on the complete benchmark set with 95% bootstrap intervals. Spearman correlation per assay for ProteinGym, higher better. For the gnomAD analysis, enrichment of rare over common variants in the deleterious tail at a threshold giving 30 false discoveries, higher better, plus mean minor allele frequency by quantile bin. For rare variant association testing, the number of significant genes at family-wise error rate below 0.05 and the number replicating larger studies, higher better.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: PhyloP and PhastCons at vertebrate, mammal and primate timescales; CADD v1.7; GPN-MSA; Nucleotide Transformer 2.5B multispecies; Evo 2 at 7B and 40B; ESM-1b, ESM-2 and ESM-3-open; Enformer, Borzoi and AlphaGenome; AlphaMissense and PrimateAI-3D; PromoterAI, SpeciesLM and GPN-Promoter; and Roulette mutation rate estimates. Scores were largely taken precomputed from the original publications or from TraitGym.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Several, and one acknowledged conflict. Chromosome 22 is held out of the model's training and is the chromosome used for the gnomAD analyses. Controls are matched to positives on chromosome, consequence and distance to the transcription start site, and for fine-mapped variants also on LD score and allele frequency, so a score cannot win by exploiting location or frequency. Only variants scored by every compared model are included. The authors also note the opposite problem for two comparators: AlphaMissense and PrimateAI-3D use human population allele frequencies in training and so gain an advantage on ClinVar, where allele frequency defines the benign class, and they report a frequency-adjusted variant of their own model alongside. Nothing is said about whether the ClinVar or HGMD variants themselves influenced any model's training corpus beyond that.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95% confidence intervals from 1,000 class-stratified bootstrap resamples on every AUPRC, and a boxplot over 31 assays for ProteinGym showing median, mean, quartiles and whiskers. The rare variant association testing experiment is repeated with three random seeds and reported as an average with each initialisation plotted. The ablation table reports the mean and the maximum over three random initialisations. No significance tests between models are reported.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One single nucleotide variant in the human genome for the classification and enrichment tasks, with its molecular consequence from Ensembl VEP under the most severe consequence rule. For ProteinGym the unit scored is a variant but the reported value is one Spearman correlation per assay. For rare variant association testing the unit is a gene and trait pair.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human for all ten tasks on this record. The wider paper also evaluates models for mouse, chicken, fruit fly, nematode and Arabidopsis against pathogenic or lethal variant sets, but those are separate benchmarks.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Information: Evaluation Benchmarks, Homo sapiens. Paper: Results, GPN-Star for model organisms

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Only one task rests on a measurement: ProteinGym's deep mutational scanning fitness scores for 31 human proteins. The other labels are database annotations or statistical inferences: expert curation in ClinVar, OMIM and HGMD, sample frequency in COSMIC, posterior inclusion probability from GWAS fine-mapping, and population allele frequency in gnomAD.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 2 caption; Results. Supplementary Information: Evaluation Benchmarks

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Unrestricted in practice: the benchmarks compare whatever each model reads. The model under test uses whole-genome alignments and a species tree rather than a single sequence, the comparators range from single-sequence genomic language models to protein language models, sequence-to-function models trained on functional genomics data, and methods that use human population allele frequencies. The one constraint applied is that a model must produce a score for a variant for that variant to count.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot for the classification and correlation benchmarks: scores are model likelihoods or published conservation and ensemble scores, with no fitting to the benchmark labels. Two exceptions sit on top of the scores: a logistic regression used for the embedding classification analyses under leave-one-chromosome-out cross-validation, and the rare variant association testing, where the GPN-Star scores are fed as annotations into DeepRVAT, which is itself trained.

strengths.text: The control design is matched rather than random: nine controls per positive, matched on chromosome, consequence and distance to the transcription start site, with LD score and allele frequency added for fine-mapped non-coding variants, which removes the easiest shortcuts on non-coding tasks.

The comparison is run on the same variant sets for every model, with the explicit rule that a variant counts only if all compared models can score it, and the models are pinned with versions and score provenance in the supplementary methods.
strengths.source_locator: Supplementary Information: Evaluation Benchmarks and Compared models

strengths.text: The benchmark datasets themselves are released, not just the results: the Hugging Face collection holds the per-task datasets alongside the models and alignments, and the analysis code is archived on Zenodo.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Data availability and Code availability. Hugging Face collection record: items

strengths.text: An unfair advantage held by two comparators is stated rather than hidden: AlphaMissense and PrimateAI-3D use allele frequency in training while ClinVar's benign class is defined by allele frequency, and the authors add a frequency-adjusted version of their own model for that comparison.

limitations.text: The benchmarks were assembled by the authors of the model that wins them, and the paper reports GPN-Star as best or joint best on every task.

The numbers are in pictures. The AUPRC values and the per-benchmark sample sizes appear only in the Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 1 panels and their headings, so a reader cannot take a model's score, or a benchmark's size, from the text. The only per-benchmark figures in text form are in the ablation table, which compares architecture variants rather than competing models.

limitations.text: Two of the label sources are not released with the benchmark or are frozen in time: HGMD data were obtained already curated from another study (ref. 91) rather than released with this benchmark, and ClinVar is release 20220924, so the ClinVar task reflects curation as of September 2022.

The rare variant association testing result is a small average difference under a design that cannot be rerun by most readers: 402 against 383 significant genes and 353 against 338 replicating, averaged over three seeds, on UK Biobank exome data for 161,822 individuals of European ancestry, which is controlled-access and one ancestry group only.

profile.summary: The RNAGym fitness leaderboard ranks sequence models by how well their scores agree with measured deep mutational scanning fitness on non-coding RNA assays. In version 0.1.1 the metric is the signed Spearman correlation between a model's score and the measured DMS fitness, averaged within each of three ncRNA categories (ribozyme, tRNA, aptamer) and then averaged over the three categories with equal weight. It is for someone choosing an RNA or genomic language model to score ncRNA variants without task-specific training.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model's scores rank RNA variants in the same order as a wet-lab fitness measurement. The leaderboard keeps only assays whose readout reports the function of the RNA molecule itself: ribozyme cleavage, tRNA function and aptamer binding. Version 0.1.1 dropped the 37 mRNA-coding assays, because their readout is protein function, and the two mRNA-splicing assays, because their readout is a regulatory phenotype in human cells. Scores on the excluded assays are kept separately for reference.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The assays come from published deep mutational scanning experiments, one row each in the repository's reference sheet with an RNA type, the wild-type construct sequence, a description of the assay and, where one exists, a PDB structure and an Rfam family. The v0.1.1 leaderboard uses the three ncRNA categories: 26 ribozyme assays, 3 tRNA assays and 2 aptamer assays. Processed assay data, raw assay data, alignments, 3D structures, cross-validation splits for supervised use and the baselines' own predictions are distributed as separate downloads, and the data are also published as a Hugging Face dataset under CC BY 4.0.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model supplies one score per variant. Within an assay the score is correlated with the measured DMS fitness by Spearman correlation, keeping the sign, so a negative entry means the model ranks fit variants as unfit. Assay values are averaged within each category, and the headline number is the unweighted average of the three category means. All masked language models on the v0.1.1 board are scored the same way: the masked-marginal log-likelihood ratio, masking each mutated position one at a time in the variant's own sequence and summing over the variant's mutated positions. The leaderboard page says this convention matters because 99.4% of the ncRNA variants carry more than one mutation, and that RiNALMo and RNA-FM were rescored to reach it.

profile.summary: This is one prospective cohort study's evaluation of a single commercial test, not a reusable suite. Plasma microbial cell-free DNA metagenomic sequencing (mcfDNA-Seq) was run on leftover plasma from children and young people treated for high-risk leukaemia at one hospital, and asked whether it names the organism a blood culture would later grow. The measures are predictive sensitivity in the 3 days before bloodstream infection onset, diagnostic sensitivity on the day of or after diagnosis, and specificity in control samples from the same patients when they had no fever or infection. It tells a reader how far ahead of a positive culture a plasma sequencing test can call the pathogen, and at what false-positive cost.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Summary, Background and Methods; Methods, Procedures and Outcomes

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a plasma sequencing test can detect the causative organism of a bloodstream infection before the patient has symptoms, which is what a pre-emptive treatment strategy would need. The authors state that no validated screening test exists for this. Three quantities are reported: predictive sensitivity over day minus 3 to day minus 1, diagnostic sensitivity over day 0 to day 1, and specificity in control samples, where specificity means that no bacterium or yeast was reported at all.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Summary, Background; Methods, Procedures and Outcomes

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Leftover clinical plasma was collected prospectively, up to once a day, from patients under 25 receiving leukaemia care at St Jude Children's Research Hospital between 9 August 2017 and 28 February 2022, who were at high risk of bloodstream infection and expected to stay at least 7 days. Blood collected for routine haematology was held at 4 degrees C, processed to plasma and frozen at minus 80 degrees C. A bloodstream infection was defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network laboratory-confirmed classification, with onset set at the collection time of the first positive blood culture. Samples from 7 days before to 1 day after onset were tested, with up to two control samples per episode from patients with no fever or infection within 7 days either side. 158 participants were enrolled; of 127 bloodstream infection episodes, 94 in 60 participants had at least one evaluable sample, and there were 162 evaluable control episodes. 19 episodes had already been reported in the study's pilot phase, and the numbers here are consolidated across both phases.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Study design and participants, Procedures; Results. ClinicalTrials.gov record: design and status modules

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Testing was done in one accredited laboratory (Karius, Redwood City, California), which reported, for each organism found against a proprietary reference genome database, a DNA fragment concentration in molecules per microlitre of plasma. Samples were tested in batches and the laboratory was masked to whether a sample came from an infection episode or a control. An episode counts as a hit only if every culture-confirmed organism was detected, including in polymicrobial episodes, which is why polymicrobial infections score lower. Each episode was treated as an independent event. The study followed Simon's optimal two-stage design with a favourable sensitivity of 50% and a target of 100 evaluable episodes, and results are given both on raw data and with logical imputation of missing values. Exploratory analyses restricted results to bacteria or to common bloodstream infection pathogens, which are the genera accounting for more than 1% of central line-associated bloodstream infections in children with cancer in a national database, and applied a post-hoc concentration cutoff of 140 molecules per microlitre chosen from a receiver operating characteristic analysis with an area under the curve of 0.73.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures, Outcomes and Statistical analysis; Results

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: Consolidated predictive sensitivity over day minus 3 to minus 1 was 51.9% (95% CI 40.5 to 63.1) across all episodes, from 42 positives among 81 evaluable episodes, and 53.8% (42.2 to 65.2) for bacterial infections. Diagnostic sensitivity on day 0 or 1 was 81.3% (71.0 to 89.1), from 65 of 80 evaluable episodes, and 83.1% (72.9 to 90.7) for bacterial infections. Sensitivity was lowest at day minus 7 and rose daily towards diagnosis. Specificity in the 162 control episodes was 82.7% (76.0 to 88.2) for any organism, 88.9% (83.0 to 93.3) when restricted to common bloodstream infection pathogens, and 93.8% (88.9 to 97.0) with both that restriction and the 140 molecules per microlitre cutoff. Sensitivity was higher in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia than acute myeloid leukaemia (adjusted odds ratio 11.1, 1.7 to 74.2) and lower in polymicrobial infections (0.0, 0.0 to 0.2). Clinical false positives were associated with gastrointestinal disturbance alone (p=0.037) and with gastrointestinal disturbance plus recent high-dose cytarabine (p=0.012). Of 80 episodes with an evaluable sample at diagnosis, 29 (36%) carried an extra organism not grown in culture, but an untreated organism was detected in only 8 (10%).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Tables 2 and 3; Summary, Findings

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One cohort at one hospital. 158 participants enrolled, 94 evaluable bloodstream infection episodes in 60 participants out of 127 episodes, and 162 evaluable control episodes. Table 2 gives the evaluable counts per analysis: 81 episodes for the predictive period and 80 for the diagnostic period on raw data, 91 of the 94 episodes being bacterial. The registry records 160 participants as the actual enrolment.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Table 2. ClinicalTrials.gov record: enrollmentInfo

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: There is no train and test split: this is a diagnostic accuracy study, and every evaluable sample contributes to the estimate. The division is by time window relative to culture-confirmed onset (day minus 7 to minus 4, day minus 3 to minus 1, day 0 to 1) and by case against control. Results are also reported as a pilot phase and a completion phase, consolidated here; the 140 molecules per microlitre cutoff was derived from the consolidated data after the fact rather than on a held-out set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures and Statistical analysis; Results

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals, higher better. Predictive sensitivity is the proportion of evaluable episodes with at least one predictive sample in which every organism grown in blood culture was also detected by mcfDNA-Seq in at least one sample from that window; diagnostic sensitivity is the same over day 0 to 1; specificity is the proportion of control samples with no bacterium or yeast reported. A generalised linear mixed model gives adjusted odds ratios for clinical factors.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures and Statistical analysis; Tables 2 and 3

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: No comparator workflow was run. The reference standard is clinical blood culture, collected from all lumens of indwelling central venous catheters and, at clinician discretion, peripheral blood, in patients with new fever or clinical concern. The only external comparison is in the Research in context panel, which cites two small earlier studies with 16 predictive episodes each reporting predictive sensitivity of 87.5% in adults in intensive care and 75.0% in children with leukaemia, the latter being this study's own pilot phase. The study's prespecified favourable sensitivity of 50% acts as the threshold the result is judged against.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures and Statistical analysis; Research in context, Evidence before this study

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Masking rather than data separation, as suits a diagnostic study. The testing laboratory was masked to whether a sample was from an infection episode or a control, and samples were tested in batches. Control samples were required to have no fever or infection within 7 days either side. The organism definition and the onset time come from an external classification (National Healthcare Safety Network) rather than from the test under evaluation. The 140 molecules per microlitre cutoff, by contrast, was derived from the same consolidated data it is then reported on.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95% confidence intervals on every sensitivity and specificity, and on the adjusted odds ratios; p values for the clinical false-positive associations. Each result is also given twice, on raw data and with logical imputation of missing values, which is the study's way of showing the effect of missing samples: for example predictive sensitivity 51.9% raw against 51.2% imputed. There are no replicate runs of the assay, and the paper notes no missing data for the variables in the mixed model.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Tables 2 and 3; Results; Methods, Statistical analysis

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A bloodstream infection episode for the sensitivity measures, scored from the plasma samples available in a time window, and a control episode or sample for specificity. The paper also reports per-day results, where the unit is a single plasma sample on a given day relative to onset.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human patients, with bacterial and fungal pathogens as the detection targets. 91 of the 94 episodes were bacterial; specificity for any organism is defined over bacteria and yeast and excludes Burkholderia species, moulds, viruses and parasites. Participants were people younger than 25 receiving leukaemia therapy.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 2 and Table 3 footnotes; Methods, Study design and participants

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Plasma microbial cell-free DNA metagenomic sequencing, run as a commercial clinical test by Karius in an accredited laboratory, which reports each organism's DNA fragment concentration in molecules per microlitre against a proprietary reference genome database. The comparator measurement is clinical blood culture. Plasma came from leftover clinical haematology samples.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: A plasma sample, and nothing else at the point of the test: the laboratory was masked to sample status, so no clinical context was available to it. Clinical variables (leukaemia type, counts, gastrointestinal disturbance, cytarabine, transplant) enter only the later modelling of what drives sensitivity and false positives, not the detection itself.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: None of the machine learning kind: the test is a fixed commercial assay with a proprietary database and was not trained or tuned on this cohort. The only parameter fitted to these data is the post-hoc 140 molecules per microlitre reporting cutoff, chosen from a receiver operating characteristic analysis of the consolidated results.

strengths.text: The design is prospective, registered and masked: samples were collected daily in advance of any infection, the study is registered as NCT03226158, and the testing laboratory did not know which samples came from infection episodes.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Study design and participants and Procedures. ClinicalTrials.gov record

strengths.text: The success criterion is strict and stated in advance: every culture-confirmed organism in an episode had to be detected, the predictive window was defined a priori, and the target sensitivity of 50% and sample size of 100 episodes were set by a two-stage design before the data were read.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures and Statistical analysis

strengths.text: Every headline figure carries a confidence interval and is reported both on raw data and with imputation for missing samples, and the exploratory cuts (bacteria only, common pathogens, concentration cutoff) are labelled as exploratory or post-hoc.

limitations.text: One assay and no comparator. The test is a single commercial product whose reference database is proprietary, so a reader cannot tell which part of performance comes from the laboratory process, the database or the reporting threshold, and no alternative workflow was run on the same samples.

One centre and one patient group: people under 25 treated for leukaemia at a single hospital, with study disruptions for staffing in 2018 to 2019 and for pandemic restrictions in 2020. Predictive sensitivity also differed sharply by leukaemia type, so the pooled figure should not be read as applying to every patient.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Study design and participants; Results

limitations.text: Nothing can be re-run or re-analysed by a third party. The study protocol is in the appendix, but individual participant data are not available, and no sequencing data, code or sample-level table is released.

The concentration cutoff that gives the best specificity was derived from the same consolidated data it is reported on, so the 93.8% figure is not an out-of-sample estimate. Specificity also depends on a definition that excludes Burkholderia species, moulds, viruses and parasites.
