profile.summary: This record covers the evaluation reported in the ENIGMA BRCA1 and BRCA2 Variant Curation Expert Panel's 2024 specification paper. The panel reviewed every ACMG/AMP classification criterion for its relevance to BRCA1 and BRCA2, used statistical methods to calibrate how strong each data type's evidence is, and then tested the resulting specifications on a pilot set of 40 variants that already had ClinVar classifications. The measure of success is how many of those variants the specifications resolve or classify with more confidence. It is useful to anyone who wants to know how a gene-specific ACMG/AMP specification is built and validated, rather than to anyone comparing computational predictors.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Summary

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things. First, whether each ACMG/AMP criterion can be applied to BRCA1 and BRCA2 at all, and at what strength: the panel found that the original descriptions of 13 evidence codes were non-applicable or overlapped other criteria, and that eight codes needed their scenario of use extended or repurposed. Second, whether the resulting specifications change classification outcomes in practice, tested on variants whose existing ClinVar status was known.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Summary

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The panel is a ClinGen Variant Curation Expert Panel that grew out of an ENIGMA BRCA1 and BRCA2 classification sub-group formed in 2015 as a ClinGen external expert panel, and became an internal panel to fit the Food and Drug Administration recognised process for ClinVar submissions. The pilot set is 40 variants chosen by their pre-existing ClinVar classification: 13 of uncertain significance or conflicting, 14 pathogenic or likely pathogenic and 13 benign or likely benign. How the calibration itself was done, and how the pilot variants were selected within each class, is in the article body, which is not in the record read.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Summary

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The pilot is scored by classification outcome, not by a continuous metric: for each of the 40 variants, whether applying the specifications resolved an uncertain or conflicting classification, and whether confidence in an already classified variant was retained or improved. The headline result is that 11 of the 13 uncertain or conflicting variants were resolved. Alongside this, the calibration step assigned evidence strengths and weights to every code using statistical methods, and the documentation was revised after the pilot for clarity and ease of use. The statistical method, the thresholds it produced and the tables holding them are in the article body and were not readable here.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Summary

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One pilot set of 40 BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants with pre-existing ClinVar classifications: 13 uncertain significance or conflicting, 14 pathogenic or likely pathogenic, 13 benign or likely benign. The data types behind each evidence code were also reviewed and calibrated, but the record read does not name or size those datasets.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Inapplicable as a train and test split: this is an expert specification applied to a pilot set, with no model and no held-out partition. The only division is by the variants' pre-existing ClinVar class, which sets up the three outcomes reported. How the calibration datasets relate to the pilot variants is not stated in the record read.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Classification outcome counts, not a continuous score: how many uncertain or conflicting variants were resolved (11 of 13) and whether confidence was retained or improved for the rest. The calibration step produced evidence strengths and weights per code; the record read does not give the quantity those were calibrated against.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The comparison points are human and procedural rather than computational: the baseline ACMG/AMP criteria as originally written, the panel's own pre-existing ENIGMA research classification process, and the variants' pre-existing ClinVar classifications. The record read states that aligning the research process with the ACMG/AMP guidelines exposed gaps in both.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: It may be in a source that could not be read. The pilot variants had pre-existing ClinVar classifications, so the panel knew the prior answer when applying the specifications, but whether curators were blinded, and whether the pilot variants were excluded from the calibration data, is not stated in the record read. The article body was not available.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Summary; the article body is not in the PMC record

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Not in the record read. The Summary says statistical methods were used to calibrate evidence strength but gives no interval, replicate or sensitivity analysis, and the pilot outcome is reported as a count of 11 of 13. Any uncertainty on the calibrated thresholds would be in the article body, which could not be read.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Summary; the article body is not in the PMC record

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One germline sequence variant in BRCA1 or BRCA2, classified under the ACMG/AMP framework. For the specification work itself, the unit is an evidence code: 13 whose original descriptions were judged non-applicable or overlapping, and eight whose scenario of use was extended or repurposed.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human. The work concerns germline variants in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 hereditary breast and ovarian cancer genes.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Not named in the record read. The Summary says only that evidence strength was calibrated for different data types, without listing them.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Summary; the article body is not in the PMC record

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Whatever the specified evidence codes permit, which the record read does not enumerate. This is an expert curation framework rather than a prediction task, so there is no restriction on inputs comparable to a model benchmark; the specification defines which evidence types may be used and at what strength.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Summary; the article body is not in the PMC record

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Inapplicable. Nothing is trained, fitted or tuned on examples in the sense a model benchmark means: the panel calibrated evidence weights by statistical analysis and then applied the written specifications by expert review, revising the documentation after the pilot.

strengths.text: Evidence strength was calibrated statistically rather than assigned by convention, and the panel reports that this calibration was what justified the utility and strength of each data type for gene-specific use.

The specifications were piloted before release, on a deliberately mixed set of 40 variants spanning uncertain or conflicting, pathogenic and benign prior classifications, and the documentation was revised in response.

The review was willing to find fault with both inputs: it reports gaps in the panel's own pre-existing research process as well as in the baseline ACMG/AMP criteria, and judged 13 evidence codes non-applicable or overlapping.

limitations.text: The pilot is 40 variants, two genes and one expert panel, so the reported resolution rate rests on 13 uncertain or conflicting variants. It is a demonstration that the specifications work, not a measurement of how often they resolve uncertainty at scale.

The panel evaluated its own specifications on variants whose prior ClinVar classifications were known, and the record read says nothing about blinding or about whether the pilot variants were independent of the calibration data.

Nothing here is reusable as a benchmark: there is no score, no held-out set, no code and no released evaluation data. The outcome is a written specification, which the authors describe as publicly accessible protocols for genetic diagnosis.

The article is not open access. The copyright line reserves all rights, including for text and data mining and AI training, and no open full text could be retrieved, so this page rests on the Summary alone.

profile.summary: This is Rewire's own study, not a third-party suite. One Evo 2 7B container image, pinned by digest, scored the 3,893 BRCA1 single nucleotide variants of the Findlay et al. saturation genome editing table on three cloud GPUs, and the resulting zero-shot loss-of-function scores were compared with CADD, mammalian phyloP and a consequence rule on the same variants. Alongside the AUROCs it records what each run cost, how much GPU memory it used, how fast it scored, and whether different hardware gives the same per-variant numbers. It answers an operational question rather than a biological one: can this model be run reproducibly on commercial clouds, and does the hardware change the answer.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three things at once. First, whether a pinned Evo 2 7B workload runs at all on each platform, gated by a correctness test that reproduces Arc's expected forward-pass loss of 0.3476563 within 0.001. Second, how well the model's zero-shot score separates loss-of-function from functional BRCA1 variants, overall and split into coding and noncoding, against three baselines that need no GPU. Third, the operational facts a clinical informatician would ask for: GPU memory, wall time, throughput, cost, and whether two machines give the same per-variant score. The authors state the point of the study is an executable recipe rather than another benchmark.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Everything is pinned and public. The container is built from NVIDIA's PyTorch 25.04 image with evo2 0.6.0 and vtx 1.1.0 and referenced by digest; the weights are Hugging Face revisions with SHA-256 checks before loading, which the authors require because Arc's loader uses pickle; the inputs come from a pinned Arc commit and are hash-checked rather than redistributed. The variant set is the Findlay et al. 2018 BRCA1 saturation genome editing table: 3,893 single nucleotide variants labelled FUNC (2,821), INT (249) or LOF (823), with consequence, a CADD score and mammalian phyloP in the same table. W1 scores each variant in an 8,192 base pair window centred on it, as the Arc notebook does, taking the variant's mean log-likelihood minus the reference's. Labels are LOF against FUNC plus INT.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: AUROC of the negated score, with 95% intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples at seed 7, resampling positions and keeping the three variants at a position together. Each baseline is compared with Evo 2 by a paired bootstrap difference in AUROC with its own interval, and no significance threshold is applied. Cross-platform agreement is measured against a reference platform as the maximum and median absolute difference in per-variant scores, the Spearman correlation, and how many variants move more than 1% of the list in rank; W4 repeats the first 200 variants in a second process on the same machine to separate run-to-run from cross-hardware variation. Each platform runs once from a clean committed revision with the same image digest, outputs are committed as evidence, and failed attempts are kept. results.json holds only scientific outputs; timings and costs live in operations.json and are not compared.
sections.source_locator: protocol.md: Metrics and uncertainty, Analysis plan and stopping conditions, Reproduction and tolerances

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: Evo 2 7B reached AUROC 0.875 (95% CI 0.859 to 0.891) over all 3,893 variants, 0.840 on coding and 0.953 on noncoding. Against the baselines in the same table, the paired differences favour Evo 2 overall (CADD 0.804, phyloP 0.781, consequence rule 0.769), but on coding variants the difference against CADD is -0.0008 with an interval from -0.026 to 0.023, so no advantage is detected there, while on noncoding the advantage holds against all three. The two H100 platforms, on different clouds, produced identical scores (maximum absolute difference 0.0, Spearman 1.0), while the L40S differed (maximum 1.3e-3, median 1.2e-4, Spearman 0.983) and its AUROC came out at 0.877 instead of 0.875. Each platform repeated its own scores exactly. Throughput was 2.93 sequences per second on the Google Cloud H100 and 2.91 on the Runpod H100, against 0.61 on the L40S, with peak W1 GPU memory of about 16.8 GiB and costs of USD 4.78, 2.82 and 2.96 for the run.

sections.title: The amendment 7 follow-up
sections.body: A later analysis, planned in advance and run without a GPU, asks whether the noncoding advantage holds against current predictors rather than the CADD v1.3 column shipped with the Findlay table. It adds CADD v1.7 for GRCh37, SpliceAI as annotated in that CADD release, and REVEL for missense variants, scored on the same variants and labels with the same grouped bootstrap, and fixes in advance what counts as an advantage holding: the 95% interval of the paired difference above zero. The repository reports the answer as no: against CADD v1.3 the noncoding advantage holds, against CADD v1.7 and SpliceAI it is not detected, and on coding and missense variants CADD v1.7 and REVEL lead. The amendment also states in advance that CADD v1.7 uses SpliceAI as a feature so the two are not independent, and that REVEL may be optimistic on BRCA1 because its training data may include these variants.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository is the deliverable: a make target runs the offline input fetch, hash checks and tests, and one orchestration command launches a platform, runs the pinned image and assembles results. Each launcher creates a machine with a one-off SSH key and a three-hour limit, copies the committed code and inputs, runs the image, copies results back and deletes the machine whatever happens. Credentials are kept outside the repository and the provider quotas needed are listed. Note what this costs: scoring ran at USD 0.45 to 0.80 per 1,000 variants at October 2026 list prices, and at least 100 GB of disk is needed because the image is about 25 GB unpacked and the two 7B checkpoints are 13.8 GB and 13.0 GB.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One variant set plus two small auxiliary sets. BRCA1: the Findlay et al. 2018 saturation genome editing table, 3,893 single nucleotide variants labelled FUNC 2,821, INT 249 and LOF 823, with consequence, CADD score and mammalian phyloP in the same file. Also chromosome 17 of GRCh37 as the sequence context, 122 labelled exon and non-exon positions from Arc's exon classifier notebook, Arc's four forward-pass test sequences, and synthetic DNA generated from seed 20261007 for the memory probe.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: There is none: the model is used zero-shot, so every one of the 3,893 variants is scored and included in the AUROC. The only partitions are for reporting: coding (missense, nonsense, synonymous) against noncoding (all other consequences), and in the bootstrap, resampling by genomic position so that the three variants at a position stay together.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC of the negated Evo 2 score for LOF against FUNC plus INT, higher better, with 95% bootstrap intervals and paired differences against each baseline. The exon workload reports AUROC on 122 positions. The operational measures are sequences per second and peak GPU memory, plus wall times and cost in US dollars; agreement is reported as maximum and median absolute score difference, Spearman correlation and rank movement.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three that need no GPU, all taken from the same Findlay table: the CADD score, mammalian phyloP (treated as higher means more conserved means predicted loss of function), and a consequence rule ordering nonsense and canonical splice above splice region above missense above other. The amendment 7 follow-up adds CADD v1.7, SpliceAI and REVEL on the same variants. No other foundation model is run.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Little is possible and the study says so. Evo 2 7B is used zero-shot on a published variant table, and nothing is stated about whether BRCA1 or these variants appear in the model's pretraining data. Where a control was impossible the study marks the result as a demonstration rather than an evaluation: the exon classifier's training data may include the 122 positions, so that workload is labelled a pipeline demonstration. Amendment 7 records in advance that REVEL's training data may include BRCA1 variants, and that CADD v1.7 and SpliceAI are not independent of each other.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Workloads, W2. amendment-007.md: Caveats stated in advance

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95% intervals from 2,000 grouped bootstrap resamples at seed 7 on every AUROC, and a paired bootstrap interval on each difference from a baseline, with no significance thresholds applied. Hardware variation is measured rather than assumed: the same 200 variants are rescored in a second process on each platform (maximum absolute difference 0.0 and Spearman 1.0 on all three), and cross-platform differences are reported against the reference platform. Each platform ran once, which the protocol says makes the timings receipts rather than a performance benchmark.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a single nucleotide variant in BRCA1, scored in an 8,192 base pair window centred on it, with a functional class from the saturation genome editing assay. For the exon workload the unit is one genomic position out of 122, and for the memory probe it is one synthetic sequence of a given length.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human, and one gene. All variants are in BRCA1 on human chromosome 17, GRCh37, and the exon positions come from the same human notebook data.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Saturation genome editing of BRCA1, from Findlay et al. 2018, which assigns each variant a functional class (FUNC, INT or LOF) used here as the label. No new experiment was performed; the study is computational and uses the published table.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only for the scoring workload: a reference window and the same window carrying the variant, 8,192 base pairs, scored with batch size 1 and mean reduction. The embedding workload reads the final-token embedding of layer blocks.26 for forward and reverse sequences. The baselines read precomputed columns (CADD, phyloP) or the annotated consequence, not sequence.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot for the variant scoring: no fitting to the BRCA1 labels, only the likelihood difference between the variant and reference windows. The exon workload is a linear-probe style setup using a separately trained classifier on frozen embeddings, and because that classifier may have seen the positions, the study treats it as a demonstration. No checkpoint is fine-tuned.

profile.summary: This is the evaluation in the FramePool paper, not a released suite. Two massively parallel reporter assay test sets of 5' UTR sequences with measured mean ribosome load are used to compare frame pooling against the published Optimus 5-Prime models: one of 20,000 random sequences all 50 nucleotides long, and one of 7,600 random sequences of 25 to 100 nucleotides. The same two length settings are also reported on truncated human 5' UTRs measured in the same experiment. Scores are Pearson correlations between predicted and observed mean ribosome load, and the point of the comparison is how well a model generalises to sequences longer than those it was trained on.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How accurately a model predicts mean ribosome load, a proxy for translation rate, from a 5' UTR sequence, and in particular whether it still works on sequences longer than its training data. The question matters because the earlier Optimus models learn position-specific weights relative to the start codon, so longer UTRs must be truncated: by the authors' count of GENCODE v19, only 30% of human 5' UTRs are 100 nucleotides or shorter and the median is about 200, so truncation usually throws away more than half the sequence.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; Results, Modelling 5'UTR of any length using frame pooling

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The data come from the Sample et al. reporter assay, not from this study. More than 200,000 entirely random 50-nucleotide 5' UTRs were fused to an enhanced green fluorescent protein coding sequence and their mean ribosome load measured by polysome profiling, with a second library of about 80,000 random UTRs of varying length. The test sets are the held-out sets from that study: 20,000 sequences of 50 nucleotides, and 7,600 sequences of 25 to 100 nucleotides with 100 per length. Of the 260,000 sequences in the fixed-length library, 20,000 were withheld as a validation set used for hyperparameters and early stopping and not for testing. The human comparison uses human 5' UTRs that were measured in the same reporter experiment, truncated to the two length settings.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Methods, Model training and Model testing; Results

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model predicts mean ribosome load for each test sequence and the score is the Pearson correlation with the measured value; the comparison is made against the Optimus models' published numbers on the same held-out sets. Training uses the Adam optimizer with mean squared error loss and early stopping after three epochs without validation improvement, keeping the model with the lowest validation error, while the variable-length and combined models were trained for six epochs straight with no early stopping. Alongside the two main models the authors train frame-unaware controls (global pooling and two dilated convolution variants on the same training set) and k-mer random forests, including one given frame-separated k-mer counts, to separate the benefit of frame information from the benefit of deep learning.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Evaluating frame pooling on MPRA data; Methods, Model training, Frame unaware deep learning models and Random forest models

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: On the 50-nucleotide random test set the two models are level: FramePool50 at 0.964 against Optimus50 at 0.966. On the 25 to 100 nucleotide random test set Optimus50 falls to 0.743 while FramePool50 holds 0.901, close to Optimus100's 0.915, which was trained on variable-length data. The human sequences follow the same pattern: 0.882 for FramePool50 against 0.889 for Optimus50 at 50 nucleotides, and 0.871 against 0.7 at 25 to 100 nucleotides. The authors read this as frame pooling giving up almost nothing in the fixed-length setting while generalising to longer sequences.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository, download the Zenodo deposit, put its data dictionary in the Data directory and run the training notebook; to reproduce the paper's plots without rerunning predictions, unpack the prediction archive into Data/Predictions and run the validation notebook. For predicting on new sequences the model is published through the Kipoi model zoo, with a dataloader that takes a BED file of 5' UTR exon regions, a VCF of variants and a reference FASTA, injects each variant and reports the log2 fold change in predicted mean ribosome load, plus the same figure for a simulated frameshift.

Random variable length: 7,600 test sequences of 25 to 100 nucleotides, 100 per length; the FramePool100 training set is 76,319 sequences. profile.summary: This is the evaluation published with OncoVI, a Python tool that automates the ClinGen, CGC and VICC oncogenicity guidelines for somatic variants. OncoVI's classifications are compared against four reference sets: 93 variants supplied by the guideline authors, 7,802 real-world variants from the Erlangen Molecular Tumor Board, 691 ClinVar variants with curated oncogenicity classifications, and a 135-variant subset of the tumour board variants that three expert cancer biologists reclassified under the guidelines. Every comparison is a three-class agreement rate between OncoVI and the reference. It shows how far an automated reading of the guidelines matches guideline authors, a tumour board and ClinVar.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and Methods, the four data set sections; Results

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether software can apply the oncogenicity guidelines and reach the same class a human assessor would. For each variant OncoVI collects evidence from public resources, decides which of the 11 oncogenic and five benign criteria are triggered, sums their points and maps the total to a class: 10 or more is oncogenic, 6 to 9 likely oncogenic, 0 to 5 a variant of uncertain significance, minus 1 to minus 6 likely benign, and minus 7 or lower benign. The comparisons then ask how often that class matches the guideline authors' own classification, a tumour board's assessment of protein function, ClinVar's curated oncogenicity call, and a blinded expert reclassification under the same guidelines.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, first paragraph. Repository: README.md, figure caption

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Four sets, each with a different reference. The standard operating procedure set is 93 variants taken from Supplementary Tables 1 and 3 of the guideline paper, with the triggered criteria, scores and classifications as the authors published them; genomic coordinates for 23 of them had to be derived by hand from the DNA change. The tumour board set is 7,802 unique somatic variants across 489 genes from 557 people seen by the Comprehensive Cancer Center Erlangen-EMN tumour board between February 2022 and February 2024, sequenced from formalin-fixed tissue with the TruSight Oncology 500 assay and classified into five classes by three expert cancer biologists. The ClinVar set is the 691 somatic variants, out of 6,113, that had an NCBI-curated oncogenicity classification as of 12 April 2025. The validation set is 135 tumour board variants chosen after the fact from the confusion matrix, taking every strong disagreement plus random variants from selected cells, which the same three experts then reclassified under the guidelines while blinded to how OncoVI implements the criteria.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Standard Operating Procedure Data Set, Molecular Tumor Board Data Set, Validation Data Set, ClinVar Data Set; Results

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Variants are annotated by a Python pipeline built on Ensembl VEP version 111.0 against GRCh38, with the dbNSFP 4.5a and SpliceAI plugins, keeping only coding consequences, dropping variants with a global gnomAD frequency of 0.025 or more, and preferring the MANE canonical transcript. OncoVI then queries the knowledgebases behind each criterion and produces a class. For scoring, the five classes are collapsed to three (oncogenic or likely oncogenic, uncertain, benign or likely benign) and compared with the reference as accuracy or concordance, with per-class sensitivity, confusion matrices, and stratification by gene class and by functional consequence. Scores assigned by OncoVI and by the reference are compared by correlation on the variants where the classes agree.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Variant Annotation via the VEP-Based In-House Pipeline and Data Analysis and Statistical Analysis; Results

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: On the guideline authors' 93 variants OncoVI reached 81% accuracy (75 of 93), with sensitivity 88% (38 of 43) for oncogenic or likely oncogenic and 83% (10 of 12) for benign or likely benign, and the scores correlated with the guideline authors' at r = 0.87. On the 7,802 tumour board variants the three-class concordance was 78% (6,060 of 7,802), which breaks down as 97% for uncertain variants (3,955 of 4,092) but 43% for benign or likely benign (961 of 2,261). On the 691 ClinVar variants it was 83% (573 of 691), with sensitivity 84% (362 of 431) for oncogenic or likely oncogenic and no variant crossing between the oncogenic and benign extremes. The validation set is the striking one: the experts' guideline-based reclassification agreed with the earlier tumour board assessment for only 34% of the 135 variants (46 of 135), and OncoVI agreed with the tumour board on 22% (30 of 135) but with the experts' reclassification on 80% (108 of 135).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Performance on the SOP, MTB and ClinVar data sets and Comparative Analysis with Expert Re-Assessment

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: OncoVI is distributed as a repository with a conda setup, a resource preparation script, a VEP installation path and an example input. It supports GRCh38 only, takes variants as text or VCF, and writes a tab-delimited Excel file holding the annotation fields, the variant-specific score, the classification and the triggered criteria. The repository also ships OncoVI_mod, a version that avoids the licensed OncoKB resource by defining oncogene and tumour suppressor roles from COSMIC instead.
sections.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Get started, Test OncoVI on an exemplary set of variants and OncoVI_mod. Paper: Results

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Four. SOP set: 93 somatic variants from the guideline authors, classified by them as 14 oncogenic, 29 likely oncogenic, 38 uncertain, 6 likely benign and 6 benign. Molecular Tumor Board set: 7,802 unique somatic variants across 489 genes from 557 individuals. ClinVar set: 691 somatic variants across 227 genes with an NCBI oncogenicity classification, out of 6,113 candidates, comprising 1 benign, 1 likely benign, 373 likely oncogenic, 58 oncogenic and 258 uncertain. Validation set: 135 tumour board variants across 104 genes, reclassified by three experts.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, the four data set sections; Results

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: None in the machine learning sense: OncoVI is a rule implementation, so every variant in every set is scored and compared, with no training or held-out portion. The only derived subset is the 135-variant validation set, which was selected after the fact from the tumour board confusion matrix: all variants with the strongest disagreement plus randomly chosen variants from the cells where OncoVI said uncertain or oncogenic.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Validation Data Set; Results

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Three-class agreement, higher better: accuracy or concordance between OncoVI's class and the reference's, reported as a percentage with the counts, plus per-class sensitivity and a confusion matrix. Correlation between OncoVI's variant-specific score and the reference's score is reported for the variants where the classes agree. Agreement is also stratified by gene class (oncogene against tumour suppressor) and by functional consequence.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: No other software is compared. The reference points are human: the guideline authors' own published classifications, the tumour board's five-class assessment of protein function, ClinVar's NCBI-curated oncogenicity classification, and three expert cancer biologists reclassifying under the guidelines. The repository adds an internal comparison between OncoVI and OncoVI_mod, which drops the licensed OncoKB resource, reported in a separate document rather than in the paper.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, the data set sections; Results. Repository: README.md, OncoVI_mod

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Blinding on the one comparison where it applies: the three experts reclassified the 135 validation variants while blinded to how OncoVI implements the criteria, although they were given the list of resources OncoVI uses for each criterion and had themselves produced the original tumour board classification. For the other three sets no control applies, because OncoVI is a rule implementation with no training data. The criteria were, however, interpreted by the OncoVI authors where the guideline text was unclear, and resources were chosen by them where the guidelines suggested none.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Validation Data Set; Results

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No intervals on the agreement rates. The paper reports counts behind every percentage, correlation coefficients with p values for the score comparisons, and Fisher exact tests for the association between triggered criteria and correct classification, with significance at p of 0.05 or below. There are no replicates: the classifications are deterministic given the resources, and resource versions are pinned in the methods rather than varied.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Analysis and Statistical Analysis; Results

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One somatic variant in a human tumour, given as genomic coordinates with reference and alternate alleles, carrying a human-assigned oncogenicity or pathogenicity class. facts.label: Assays

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Genomic coordinates on GRCh38, as a text table or a VCF, and whatever the integrated public resources return for them. The pipeline uses VEP annotation with dbNSFP and SpliceAI scores, gnomAD frequencies, ClinVar, COSMIC and, in the default configuration, the licensed OncoKB; no sequence model or structure is involved.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: None. OncoVI is a deterministic rule engine: each criterion is coded as IF-ELSE logic over the resources, points are summed and the class follows from fixed thresholds. Nothing is trained, fitted or tuned on any of the four reference sets.

strengths.text: The reference sets are of different kinds and the weak spots show up differently in each: guideline authors' own variants, a real tumour board cohort, ClinVar curation and a blinded expert reclassification.

strengths.text: Disagreements are followed up rather than left as a percentage. The validation set deliberately includes every strongest disagreement, and the paper traces where the score sat relative to a class threshold, for example that 55% of the oncogenic variants OncoVI called uncertain scored four or five, just under the cutoff.

strengths.text: Every percentage is reported with its counts, so each figure can be traced to the exact set it belongs to, and the resource and tool versions behind the annotation are pinned in the methods.

strengths.text: The code is public with a documented setup, and a variant that avoids the licensed OncoKB resource is provided so the tool can be run without it.

On the 135 validation variants the experts' guideline-based reclassification matched the same experts' earlier tumour board assessment for only 34%, so an agreement rate against the tumour board (22% here, 78% over the full cohort) measures the reference as much as the tool.

limitations.text: The 80% agreement on the validation set is not an independent estimate. That set was chosen after seeing the confusion matrix, it is enriched for disagreements, and the experts were given the resources OncoVI uses for each criterion before reclassifying.

limitations.text: Agreement is uneven across variant kinds in a way the headline figures hide: on the tumour board set the benign and likely benign class agrees at 43% against 97% for uncertain, and truncating alterations agree at 49.4% against 78.2% for missense.

profile.summary: These are the two labelled sets Brandes et al. built to test whether a protein language model can score coding variants that are not single amino acid substitutions. One holds 3,470 in-frame insertions, deletions and deletion-insertion combinations from ClinVar, 1,791 pathogenic and 1,679 benign; the other holds 36,000 or so ClinVar stop-gain variants, split by whether the new stop codon is expected to trigger nonsense-mediated decay. Both are scored by ROC-AUC for separating pathogenic from benign. They are useful to anyone asking whether a sequence model's likelihood scores transfer from missense variants to indels and truncations.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants; Fig. 6 legend. Repository: the indel benchmark table

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an effect score separates pathogenic from benign variants in two classes of coding variant that most variant effect predictors cannot handle: in-frame indels, which change the length of the protein, and stop gains, which truncate it. The authors' point is that a protein language model can be applied to any amino acid sequence, so it can score these as well as missense variants. The stop-gain set is further split by nonsense-mediated decay, because a truncation often acts at the transcript level rather than through the protein sequence a language model sees.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Both sets are drawn from ClinVar, with labels downloaded from the ClinVar variant_summary table, and the authors say only high-confidence variants were included, with the processing described in the Supplementary Methods. The published indel table holds 3,470 rows against RefSeq NM transcripts, each with the wild-type and mutated sequence, the affected window, the number of amino acids affected and the length difference, labelled 1 for 1,791 variants and 0 for 1,679; its mut_type column gives 2,248 deletions, 937 insertions and 285 delins. The stop-gain set is partitioned with the 50 base pair rule, which treats a transcript as likely to undergo decay only if the new stop codon falls more than 50 bases upstream of the last exon junction in the coding region, applied using exon annotations from the human genome.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Data availability; Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects; Fig. 6 legend. Repository: the indel benchmark table and README

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method supplies one score per variant and the whole set is treated as a single classification task, scored by global ROC-AUC rather than averaged per gene; the authors argue a global figure is more informative for clinical use because variants are compared across genes. For indels the model score is the pseudo-log-likelihood ratio between the mutated and wild-type sequences, in three variants: plain, weighted by sequence length, and absolute valued. For stop gains the score is the lowest log-likelihood ratio among all possible missense variants in the region lost after the new stop codon. Differences between methods are tested by a permutation test over 2,000 iterations, shuffling the scores between variants, with one-tailed empirical p values and a floor of p below 0.001. Uncertainty on the stop-gain figures comes from bootstrapping 140 pathogenic and 140 benign variants from each group over 20 iterations.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Generalized effect scores for indels and stop-gain variants, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification, Testing for significant performance differences

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: On the indel set the absolute-valued score reaches ROC-AUC 0.874, ahead of the plain 0.869 and the weighted 0.861, and all three beat CADD at 0.835; on delins variants alone the gap is wider, 0.887 against 0.671. The three sequence-similarity baselines are near or below 0.6: edit distance 0.501, pairwise alignment 0.586, BlastP 0.581. On stop gains, ESM1b scores 0.734 on variants not expected to undergo decay but only 0.565 on those that are, and on the non-decay group it beats the number of residues lost (0.649) and the fraction of the protein lost (0.599). The authors also estimate from the score distribution that 52% of in-frame indel variants of uncertain significance in ClinVar are pathogenic.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository publishes both benchmark tables with every method's scores already in them, so a comparison can be reproduced from the files alone. To score new variants, install the listed dependencies and run the multi-residue scoring script, which takes a CSV of wild-type sequence, mutated sequence and start position; a separate script scores all possible missense substitutions in a FASTA file, which is the route used for stop gains.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two ClinVar-derived sets. In-frame indels: 3,470 variants, 1,791 pathogenic and 1,679 benign, which the published table splits into 2,248 deletions, 937 insertions and 285 delins. Stop gains: 36,034 pathogenic and 345 benign variants in the Fig. 6d legend, split into 3,672 pathogenic with 147 benign not expected to undergo nonsense-mediated decay and 32,362 pathogenic with 198 benign expected to undergo it.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 6 legend. Repository: the indel benchmark table, label and mut_type columns

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train, validation or test split: each set is evaluated whole as a single classification task, which the authors can do because the method is unsupervised. The only partitioning is by variant class for reporting: deletions, insertions and delins for the indel set, and the 50 base pair decay rule for the stop-gain set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification; Discussion; Fig. 6 legend

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Global ROC-AUC on pathogenic versus benign, higher better, computed over the whole set rather than averaged per gene. Elsewhere in the paper a label-balanced PRC-AUC is also used, obtained by downsampling each class to 80% of the minority class 100 times and averaging, but the indel and stop-gain figures are reported as ROC-AUC.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification; Results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: On indels, one published predictor and three simple scores: CADD, plus Levenshtein edit distance, a pairwise alignment score (match 2, mismatch minus 1) and BlastP with BLOSUM62 and gap penalties. On stop gains, no published predictor at all, and three simple scores: number of residues lost, percentage of residues lost, and the binary 50 base pair rule. The authors state why: nearly all indel and stop-gain predictors are trained on clinical databases, which would make evaluation on ClinVar circular, and CADD is the exception they could use.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The main control is the choice of comparators, not a data split. Because the evaluated method is unsupervised, the authors argue there is no leakage from training into these ClinVar sets, and they exclude predictors trained on clinical databases to avoid circularity, which is why only CADD appears on indels and nothing on stop gains. The sets themselves are restricted to high-confidence ClinVar variants. No sequence identity cut-off between the indel set and anything else is described.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Discussion; Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects; Results

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Bootstrapped standard deviations on the stop-gain figures and permutation p values on the indel comparison. For Fig. 6d, 140 pathogenic and 140 benign variants were sampled from each group over 20 iterations, and the error bars are the standard deviation of the resulting ROC-AUCs. For Fig. 6b, one-tailed p values from 2,000 permutations are reported for the difference between CADD and each ESM1b score, with p below 0.001 when no permutation matched the observed gap. No error bars are reported for the indel ROC-AUCs themselves.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification and Testing for significant performance differences; Fig. 6 legend

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One coding variant in a human protein-coding transcript, labelled pathogenic or benign. For the indel set the published row carries the wild-type and mutated protein sequence, the start and end position, the reference and alternative alleles, the number of amino acids affected and the length difference, against RefSeq NM transcripts. For the stop-gain set the variant is a substitution creating a premature stop codon.
facts.source_locator: Repository: the indel benchmark table header and seq_source column. Paper: Fig. 6 legend

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human only. The variants come from ClinVar, the scoring is against human protein isoforms, and the 50 base pair rule was applied using exon annotations in the human genome.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects; Data availability

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. The labels are clinical assertions from ClinVar, restricted to high-confidence entries, not experimental measurements. Deep mutational scanning data are used elsewhere in the same paper, but not in these two sets.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Protein sequence for the evaluated method: the wild-type and mutated amino acid sequences, with no alignment or structure. Where a sequence exceeds the model's 1,022 amino acid limit, the score is computed on a window containing the affected region with 511 residues of context before it and enough after to fill the limit. The stop-gain score needs the position of the new stop codon, and the 50 base pair rule needs exon annotations, which is transcript-level information used for the partition rather than by the model.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Generalized effect scores for indels and stop-gain variants. Repository: README.md, Usage

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot. The scores are likelihood ratios from a pretrained protein language model with no fitting to these labels; the only choices are which of the three pseudo-log-likelihood ratio forms to use for indels, and taking the minimum missense score over the lost region for stop gains. CADD, the one published comparator, is a supervised method.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results and Fig. 6 legend; Discussion

strengths.text: Both labelled sets are published as tables with every compared method's scores in them, so the reported ROC-AUCs can be recomputed without rerunning any model, and the counts check out: the indel file has 3,470 rows, 1,791 labelled 1 and 1,679 labelled 0.
strengths.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Benchmarks; the indel benchmark table. Paper: Fig. 6 legend

strengths.text: The authors exclude comparators that were trained on ClinVar rather than reporting flattering comparisons, and say so explicitly, which is why only CADD appears on indels.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

strengths.text: The stop-gain set is split by expected nonsense-mediated decay, which exposes where a protein-sequence model fails: 0.734 on variants not expected to undergo decay against 0.565 on those that are. The authors report the weak half rather than only the aggregate.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants; Fig. 6 legend

strengths.text: Simple sequence-similarity baselines are included, which gives a floor for the indel task: edit distance scores 0.501, close to chance, so the task is not solved by noticing that the sequence changed.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results and Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

limitations.text: The stop-gain set is extremely unbalanced: 345 benign against 36,034 pathogenic overall, and only 147 benign in the non-decay group that the headline 0.734 is computed on. ROC-AUC on such a set rests on a few hundred negatives, which is why the authors bootstrap 140 of each class rather than reporting a single number.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 6 legend; Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

limitations.text: Almost nothing can be compared against. On stop gains no published predictor is evaluated at all, and on indels only CADD, so these sets rank one model against three simple scores rather than against the field.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

limitations.text: The labels are clinical assertions, so the benchmark inherits ClinVar's biases, and the rule for what counts as high confidence is in the Supplementary Methods rather than the article. The stop-gain partition also depends on the 50 base pair rule being correct, which is a heuristic rather than a measurement.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

limitations.text: The two counts given for the stop-gain groups do not agree between the Fig. 6d legend and the Methods: the legend says 32,362 pathogenic in the decay group and 36,034 overall, while the bootstrapping description says 32,441 and 36,113. A user should check the published stop-gain file before quoting either.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 6 legend; Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

run_guide.summary: Get the published benchmark tables, and score new multi-residue variants with the repository's command-line tool.
prerequisites: Python with tqdm, numpy, pandas, biopython, torch and fair-esm, as the README's install line lists.
The ESM1b weights, which fair-esm downloads; the README notes the model comes from Meta AI's official repository.
For scoring a new set, a CSV with wt_seq, mut_seq and start_pos columns.
The code is MIT licensed. ClinVar labels are public; the HGMD part of the wider paper is not, but neither of these two benchmarks uses it.

steps.title: Get the code and the published benchmarks
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/ntranoslab/esm-variants.git
cd esm-variants
git checkout --detach 0c33758a5073e5d6e673d9a16a40e5b0af46851d

steps.shell: pip3 install tqdm numpy pandas biopython torch fair-esm
steps.explanation: The one install line the README gives.

steps.title: Score multi-residue variants
steps.shell: python3 esm_score_multi_residue_mutations.py --input-csv-file /path/to/input.csv --output-csv-file /path/to/output.csv
steps.explanation: The README's command for in-frame indels and other multi-residue changes. The input CSV needs wt_seq, mut_seq and start_pos; the wild-type and mutated sequences for every variant in the indel benchmark are already columns of the published table.

steps.title: Score all missense substitutions, the route used for stop gains
steps.shell: python3 esm_score_missense_mutations.py --input-fasta-file /path/to/input.fasta --output-csv-file /path/to/output.csv
steps.explanation: The README's other command. A stop-gain score in the paper is the lowest of the missense log-likelihood ratios over the region lost after the new stop codon, so this is the script that produces the underlying scores; the paper does not publish a command that performs that minimisation.
steps.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Usage. Paper: Fig. 6 legend

outputs: A CSV of effect scores for the variants given, written to the path passed to the script.
The cloned repository's benchmark tables, which already hold the ESM1b, CADD and baseline scores for the 3,470 indels and the stop-gain set, plus Table_of_results.xlsx.

No published command computes the reported ROC-AUCs, the permutation tests or the bootstrapped error bars; the repository publishes the scored tables and the scoring tools only.

The stop-gain pipeline is not a single command: the minimisation over missense scores in the lost region and the 50 base pair partition are described in the paper, not shipped as a script in the files read.

profile.summary: The Plant Genomic Benchmark (PGB) is the set of eight supervised plant genomics tasks released with AgroNT, a DNA language model trained on 48 plant genomes. The tasks cover polyadenylation sites, splice sites, long non-coding RNA, promoter strength, terminator strength, chromatin accessibility, tissue-specific gene expression and an intergenic enhancer set, over 32 datasets in the paper's Table 1 (31 in the released dataset card's size table) with sequences from 101 to 6000 base pairs. It is for comparing deep learning methods on plant sequence prediction, in a field the authors say lacked a shared benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction and Table 1. Dataset card: Dataset Overview

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model can predict functional annotations and quantitative measurements from plant DNA sequence. The eight tasks span regulatory features, RNA processing and gene expression: binary classification of polyadenylation sites, splice sites, long non-coding RNA and intergenic enhancer regions; regression on promoter and terminator strength; multi-label classification of chromatin accessibility; and multi-output regression of tissue-specific gene expression. The authors' stated aim is a shared assessment for deep learning methods in plant genomics, with attention to species that are little studied.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Table 1. Dataset card: Dataset Overview

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each task is a reuse or a rebuild of published data. Table 1 names the source of each: polyadenylation, lncRNA, gene expression and the enhancer set were compiled for this study, splice sites come from Baten et al., promoter strength from Jores et al., terminator strength from Gorjifard et al. and chromatin accessibility from Zhao et al. Polyadenylation sequences are 400 bp with the poly(A) site at position 301, and negatives were made by shifting that position by 1 to 50 bases, giving twice as many negatives as positives. The lncRNA negatives are mRNA sequences matched to each lncRNA on length and GC content. Promoter sequences are the 170 bp windows from -165 to +5 around annotated transcription start sites, measured by STARR-seq in two systems, tobacco leaves and maize protoplasts; terminators are 170 nucleotides from -150 to +20 around a cleavage and polyadenylation site, and the terminator study also added randomised sequences of varying GC content. For promoters, terminators and chromatin accessibility the authors downloaded the original studies' own train and test sets so their numbers can be compared with the original models.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a fine-tuned model's predictions on each task's held-out test split, scored with the metric the task's source study used. The authors report AUROC and AUPRC for the imbalanced classification tasks (splice sites, polyadenylation, lncRNA, chromatin accessibility), the coefficient of determination R2 for promoter and terminator strength, and for gene expression the R2 of a linear model between predicted and observed levels on held-out genes. Fine-tuning in the paper uses IA3, which injects re-scaling vectors at the model's activations and updates about 1% of the parameters. The dataset card's size table gives the train, validation and test counts for each of the 31 datasets it lists; several tasks have no validation split, and the card notes that lncRNA fine-tuning was done on all six species datasets together because each is small.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Fine-tuning strategy, Splicing site prediction, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction; Fig. 5 caption. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes

sections.title: Promoter and terminator strength tasks
sections.body: These two tasks are regression on STARR-seq activity of 170 bp sequences from Arabidopsis thaliana, Zea mays and Sorghum bicolor, measured separately in tobacco leaves and in maize protoplasts, with terminator data covering Arabidopsis thaliana and Zea mays and over 50,000 terminators. The dataset card splits each task into a leaf and a protoplast dataset: 7154 and 7595 test sequences for promoter strength, 4806 and 4811 for terminator strength. The paper reports R2 of 0.7 in the maize system and 0.73 in the tobacco system for promoters, and 0.67 and 0.77 for terminators. Figure 3e and 3f compare AgroNT with the two CNN models from the original studies across plant species: on promoters AgroNT was ahead in every species and system, by 3 R2 points on average, and on terminators it matched or beat the CNN in 5 of 6 datasets.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Promoter and terminator activity prediction; Fig. 3 caption; Methods, Promoter and terminator strength prediction. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The benchmark is distributed as a Hugging Face dataset with one configuration per dataset, loaded by name with the datasets library. The AgroNT weights are published separately on Hugging Face and through the InstaDeep nucleotide-transformer repository. No scoring script is published with the data, so the metrics have to be computed by the user, and the paper states that the pre-training code is proprietary and not released.
sections.source_locator: Dataset card: Example Usage. Paper: Data availability and Code availability

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Eight tasks. Table 1 of the paper, and the summary table on the dataset card, list 32 datasets with six for gene expression; the dataset card's size table lists 31 datasets, with five gene expression datasets (Glycine max, Oryza sativa, Solanum lycopersicum, Zea mays, Arabidopsis thaliana). Table 1 gives the number of datasets per task: polyadenylation 6, splicing site 2, lncRNA 6, promoter strength 2, terminator strength 2, chromatin accessibility 7, gene expression 6, enhancer region 1. Sequence lengths run from 170 bp (promoters and terminators) and 398 to 400 bp (splice and poly(A) sites) to 1000 bp (chromatin accessibility and enhancers) and 6000 bp (gene expression), with lncRNA sequences from 101 to 6000 bp. Test counts per dataset range from 360 (lncRNA in cassava) to 377,873 (Arabidopsis donor splice sites).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1. Dataset card: task table and Dataset Sizes

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Fixed train, validation and test counts per dataset on the dataset card, with the split rule differing by task. Polyadenylation and lncRNA test sets are restricted to sequences from a single sampled chromosome per species, with chromosomes 1A, 1B and 1D for Triticum aestivum; the splice site test set is chromosome 5 of Arabidopsis thaliana; chromatin accessibility uses the same validation and test chromosomes as the Zhao et al. study; promoter, terminator and chromatin accessibility reuse the original studies' train and test sets. Polyadenylation, splicing and lncRNA have no validation split on the card.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Per task, with higher better in every case. AUROC and AUPRC for polyadenylation, splice site, lncRNA and chromatin accessibility; the coefficient of determination R2 for promoter and terminator strength; for gene expression the R2 of a linear model between predicted and observed levels on held-out genes; AUC for the cassava intergenic enhancer set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction; Results, in silico mutagenesis; Fig. 5 caption

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The models from the source studies, task by task: two CNN models for promoter and terminator strength (Figure 3e and 3f), the Zhao et al. chromatin accessibility predictions, and lncRNA-LSTM for the Zea mays lncRNA dataset of Meng et al., where AgroNT reached an AUC of 0.991 against the reported 0.9934. The paper also compares its gene expression results with two earlier models for Arabidopsis thaliana and Zea mays and reports up to a three-fold improvement.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 3 caption; Results, lncRNA prediction and gene expression; Methods, Chromatin profiles prediction

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Chromosome-level separation on the tasks the authors built: the polyadenylation and lncRNA test sets hold only sequences from one sampled chromosome per species, and the splice site test set is chromosome 5. Chromatin accessibility reuses the validation and test chromosomes of the source study. The lncRNA negatives are matched to the positives on length and GC content so that length alone cannot solve the task. No sequence identity cut-off between train and test is described, and nothing is said about overlap between the test sequences and the 48 genomes used for pre-training.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Only for the lncRNA task. There the authors resampled the matched mRNA negatives five times per species and report the spread: the median range of the difference in AUROC across resamplings is 1.6 to 3.9 points and in AUPRC 2.5 to 4.6 points. No seeds, replicates or confidence intervals are described for the other tasks.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, lncRNA prediction; Results, lncRNA prediction

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a DNA sequence window with a label or a measured value: a 400 bp window centred on a candidate poly(A) site, a 398 bp splice site window, an lncRNA or mRNA transcript sequence, a 170 bp promoter or terminator with its STARR-seq strength, a 1000 bp window labelled for open chromatin or enhancer activity, or a 6000 bp gene-proximal window with expression levels across tissues.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction. Dataset card: task table

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Edible and model plants, plus one alga. Named across the tasks: Arabidopsis thaliana, Oryza sativa (japonica and indica), Zea mays, Sorghum bicolor, Setaria italica, Brachypodium distachyon, Glycine max, Solanum lycopersicum, Triticum aestivum, Medicago truncatula, Trifolium pratense, Manihot esculenta (cassava) and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. The promoter and terminator assays were read out in tobacco leaves and maize protoplasts rather than in the source species.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction, Promoter and terminator strength prediction. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: STARR-seq for promoter and terminator strength, ATAC-seq for chromatin accessibility, RNA-seq for tissue-specific gene expression, and PRO-seq based intergenic enhancer calls in cassava. The polyadenylation labels come from the curated PlantAPAdb catalogue of alternative polyadenylation sites, the splice site labels from an existing annotated dataset, and the lncRNA labels from the GreeNC database.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction, gene expression prediction, Polyadenylation site prediction. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes and ISM section

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only. Every task gives a fixed-length nucleotide window, and the paper's own model reads a sequence of up to about 6000 bp tokenised into 6-mers. No alignment, structure or annotation input is described as part of a task.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 1 caption. Dataset card: task table

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Supervised fine-tuning on each task's training split. The paper fine-tunes with IA3, a parameter-efficient method that updates about 1% of the model's parameters, and notes that for lncRNA the six species datasets were fine-tuned together in a single training run because each is small. The benchmark itself does not restrict the adaptation method.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Fine-tuning strategy. Dataset card: note under Dataset Sizes

strengths.text: The data are published in one place with a DOI and with per-dataset train, validation and test counts, loadable by task name, which makes the splits reusable rather than something each user rebuilds.
strengths.source_locator: Dataset card: Dataset Sizes and Example Usage. Hugging Face API record: tags

strengths.text: On the tasks the authors built, test sets are separated by chromosome rather than at random, and for the lncRNA task the negative mRNA sequences are matched to the positives on length and GC content.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction

strengths.text: Where a task comes from an earlier study, the authors kept that study's train and test sets and its metric, so a new result can be put beside the original model's.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction

strengths.text: The benchmark covers more than one model species: twelve plants and one alga appear across the tasks, including under-studied crops such as cassava, which the authors give as a reason for the work.

limitations.text: The data licence is non-commercial and share-alike: the Hugging Face repository is marked cc-by-nc-sa-4.0, so commercial use is not permitted even though the paper itself is CC BY 4.0.
limitations.source_locator: Hugging Face API record: cardData.license and tags. Dataset card: front matter

limitations.text: The benchmark was assembled by the authors of the model it was first used to evaluate, and in the paper AgroNT is the method that wins on it.

No evaluation code or leaderboard comes with the data. The dataset card gives only a loading example, the paper says the pre-training code is proprietary, and the headline comparisons in Figure 3e and 3f are figures, so a reader has to take the per-species values from the figure data files rather than from a table.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Code availability; Fig. 3 caption. Dataset card: Example Usage and Data source for Figures 2-8

limitations.text: Three tasks have no validation split on the dataset card (polyadenylation, splicing and lncRNA), so any model selection on those tasks has to come out of the training data.
