profile.summary: This is the evaluation published with MetageNN, a long-read taxonomic classifier. Six tools assign Oxford Nanopore reads from 81 verified bacterial isolates to a genus, all of them indexing the same 516 reference genomes, in two settings: when the read's own species is in the database, and when it is not. The same tools are then run on 30 pseudo-mock communities built from the out-of-database isolates, and Table 1 records each tool's database size and classification speed. It is useful to someone choosing a read classifier and wanting to know how each behaves when the species is missing from the reference set.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results summary; Methods, Test datasets and Databases; Table 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a tool can put a long read in the right genus, and what happens when the read's species has no genome in the reference database. The authors set the problem up around that gap: the SRA has Nanopore data for only 489 unique bacterial species while RefSeq had complete genomes for more than 6800, so a classifier is often asked about a species it has never seen. The second question is cost: how much disk the database needs and how many reads per second the tool classifies.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MetageNN model; Results for Species out of the database settings; Table 1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The test data are real Nanopore reads with a checked ground truth. The authors searched the SRA for R.9.4.1 Nanopore datasets from bacterial isolates whose species had a RefSeq genome, confirmed the strain name matched, then assembled each read set with Flye and two rounds of medaka polishing and required average nucleotide identity above 99% to the reference. That left 81 strains, subsampled to about 20,000 reads each. The 47 strains whose genome is in the reference set form the Species in the database set and the remaining 34 form the Species out of the database set. The main database is the 47 genomes expanded about tenfold with randomly chosen RefSeq representative genomes, giving 516 genomes across 505 species and 311 genera; the repository's list of those assemblies has 516 lines. A smaller 47-genome database was used only for model and hyperparameter choices and for the comparison against other deep learning classifiers.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Databases. Repository: data/main_database_list_of_genomes.txt

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every tool indexes the same main database, and the non-machine-learning tools are run at their default settings. Reads are classified at genus rank and scored by sensitivity, precision and F1 per bacterial isolate, then averaged across isolates within a dataset; differences against MetageNN are tested with a Wilcoxon rank sum test. Error bars in the figures are the standard deviation across isolates. MetageNN itself was trained on 8x coverage of the main database genomes, about 17 million 1 kbp sequences, with 200 validation sequences per genome, and classifies a read by splitting it into non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks and taking a majority vote, accepting a call only at probability 0.5 or above. GeNet was given a matched parameter count and the same training data so that the difference between the two is mainly how they encode a long read.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Databases; Evaluation metrics; Experimental setup; Fig. 3 caption

sections.title: The community-level test
sections.body: Thirty pseudo-mock communities were assembled from the reads of the out-of-database isolates, each with a random number of species between 20 and 34 and up to 100,000 reads log-distributed across them. Two things are reported: the percentage of reads a tool classifies, and sensitivity, precision and F1 for the presence or absence of a genus at cumulative read thresholds of 0.001%, 0.1% and 1% of the reads in the dataset, which is about 1, 100 and 1000 reads. GeNet was dropped from this comparison because of its performance in the read-level test. MetageNN classified 93.26% of the reads, ahead of MMseqs2 at 85.49%, Kraken2 at 64.90%, MEGAN-LR at 53.06% and MetaMaps at 37.30%.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis; Read classification results

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: The two settings separate the tools. When the species is in the database, Kraken2, MetaMaps and MEGAN-LR have the best average F1, sensitivity and precision and beat MetageNN. When it is not, MetageNN has the highest sensitivity along with MMseqs2, improving on MetaMaps, Kraken2, GeNet and MEGAN-LR by 100%, 23%, 17% and 36%; its precision is slightly lower than MetaMaps, Kraken2 and MMseqs2, and only the gap to MEGAN-LR is significant. Over both sets together MMseqs2 is first on F1 and sensitivity with 0.85 and 0.81, then Kraken2 with 0.83 and 0.79. Every tool does worse when three or fewer species share the tested genus. Table 1 gives database size and speed: MetageNN uses 0.839 GB at 1424 reads per second, against 3.7 GB for Kraken2, 5.1 GB for MEGAN-LR and 27.8 GB for MMseqs2.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results for all genomes; Results for Species in the database settings; Results for Species out of the database settings; Table 1

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository publishes the model code, the genome and isolate lists and the hyperparameter files, not the benchmark harness. Requirements are installed by a shell script. Sequences are turned into canonical 6-mer profiles with the Phylopythia k-mer counter, fasta2kmers2, and training is one command that reads a settings JSON. Only the small-database training set, at 1x coverage, is offered for download, through a link in the data folder; the main-database training data and the test read sets are not in the repository, only lists of the SRA identifiers and RefSeq assemblies they come from.
sections.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Requirements, Counting k-mers, Settings and Training; data/README.txt

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Three test sets plus one reference database. Species in the database: Nanopore reads from 47 bacterial isolates, about 20,000 reads each. Species out of the database: reads from the remaining 34 isolates. Mock, Species out of DB: 30 pseudo-mock communities of 20 to 34 species each with up to 100,000 reads. The shared main database holds 516 genome assemblies covering 505 species and 311 genera; the repository's list of those assemblies has 516 lines. A separate small database of the 47 genomes was used for parameter choices only.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Databases; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis. Repository: data/main_database_list_of_genomes.txt

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: The split is by whether the test species is in the reference database, not by random sampling. Training sequences are 1 kbp windows sampled from the database genomes (8x coverage of the main database, about 17 million samples; 1x coverage of the small database, about 235,000 sequences), validation is 200 sequences per genome drawn the same way with different seeds, and the test reads are real Nanopore reads from isolates. The 34 out-of-database isolates have no genome in the database at all.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Databases; Experimental setup

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Sensitivity, precision and F1 at genus rank, higher better, averaged across bacterial isolates for the read-level tests and across the 30 communities for the community-level test, where presence of a genus is decided at cumulative read thresholds of 0.001%, 0.1% and 1%. The community test also reports the percentage of reads classified, higher better. Table 1 reports database memory in GB, lower better, and speed in reads per second, higher better.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation metrics; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis; Table 1

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five classifiers beside MetageNN: MetaMaps and MEGAN-LR (alignment based, with minimap2 alignments for MEGAN-LR), MMseqs2 with a nucleotide database, Kraken2 for k-mer matching, and GeNet as the deep learning representative. DeepMicrobes and GeNet were also compared on the small database for training and inference cost and for robustness to simulated errors; GeNet was dropped from the community-level test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Baselines (both sections); Results; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two. The Species out of the database setting removes the test species' genome from the reference set altogether, and the results are further stratified by how many species share the tested genus (exactly one, two or three, more than three), which separates the easy cases from the hard ones. Within the model's own data, validation sequences are drawn with different seeds from the training sequences. Test reads are real reads whose identity was confirmed by assembly and an average nucleotide identity above 99% to the reference, so the ground truth does not come from the classifier under test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets; Results for Species out of the database settings; Experimental setup

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Spread across isolates and a significance test, but no repeated runs. Figure error bars are the standard deviation across the ONT bacterial isolates, and MetageNN is compared with each baseline by Wilcoxon rank sum test with significance marked on the figures. No seeds, repeated trainings or confidence intervals for the aggregate numbers are reported.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation metrics; Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 captions

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is an Oxford Nanopore sequencing read, classified to a genus; MetageNN works on non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks of that read and votes. For the community-level test the unit is instead a pseudo-mock community, and the call is whether a genus is present in it.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Experimental setup; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Bacteria only. 81 bacterial strains provide the reads, and the main database holds 516 bacterial genome assemblies across 505 species and 311 genera from RefSeq. No host, virus, fungus or archaeon is part of the evaluation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Databases. Repository: data/README.txt

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Oxford Nanopore whole-genome sequencing of bacterial isolates on R.9.4.1 flow cells, taken from the SRA. The labels are not an assay readout: each read's true genus follows from the isolate it was sequenced from, after the strain match was confirmed by assembly and average nucleotide identity. Simulated reads from the BadReads tool were used separately to test robustness at 95%, 90% and 80% median accuracy.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets; Experimental setup for the small-database experiments

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Nucleotide sequence and the shared reference database, nothing else. Every tool indexes the same 516 genomes; MetageNN reads only canonical 6-mer profiles of 1 kbp windows, which the authors chose because short k-mer profiles are less disturbed by sequencing errors and are read-length agnostic.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Databases and MetageNN model. Repository: README.md, Counting k-mers

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Mixed by tool, which is part of the comparison. The learned models (MetageNN, GeNet, DeepMicrobes) are trained from scratch on sequences sampled from the database genomes, with early stopping on validation loss and hyperparameters tuned on the 1x dataset; MetageNN took three days on four GPUs and GeNet about six. The alignment and k-mer tools are not trained: their indices are built from the same genomes and they run at default settings.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Experimental setup (both sections). Repository: settings/MetageNN_settings_main_database.json

strengths.text: Every tool queries the same 516-genome database and the non-learned tools run at their defaults, so the comparison is not confounded by different reference sets.
The ground truth is checked rather than assumed: each isolate's strain match was confirmed by assembling its reads and requiring average nucleotide identity above 99% to the reference genome.
The missing-genome case is tested directly and then stratified by how many species share the tested genus, which shows that all tools degrade when three or fewer references are available.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results for Species out of the database settings

strengths.text: Cost is reported beside accuracy: Table 1 gives each tool's database memory and reads per second on the same data, so a reader can see what a given accuracy costs.

limitations.text: The benchmark was designed and run by the developers of one of the tools in it, and MetageNN is the tool it is built to show, including the choice to drop GeNet from the community-level comparison.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results summary; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis

limitations.text: The reference database is small by clinical standards: 516 genomes over 505 species, where the authors note RefSeq had complete genomes for more than 6800 bacterial species. A tool's behaviour here need not carry over to a full-size index.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Databases and MetageNN model

limitations.text: Scope is narrow: bacterial isolates only, genus rank only, one sequencing chemistry (R.9.4.1 Nanopore), and the authors call the model itself a proof of concept.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Experimental setup. Repository: README.md

limitations.text: The per-tool sensitivity, precision and F1 values live only in bar plots (Figures 3 and 4), and no result table or file of them is published, so a reader cannot read exact numbers for most comparisons. The repository ships the model code and the data lists, not a runner for the benchmark, and only the 1x small-database training set is offered for download.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 captions; Availability of data and materials. Repository: README.md, Data; data/README.txt

profile.summary: The GPN paper's own check of how well its DNA language model, trained on eight Brassicales genomes, predicts held-out Arabidopsis thaliana sequence and how well its embeddings separate gene regions. It reports test perplexity on a held-out chromosome, perplexity by position class in a 1-Mb test region, and a leave-one-chromosome-out classifier of gene regions from averaged embeddings. It is useful to plant genomics researchers comparing DNA language models on A. thaliana, but only the authors' own models are scored.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, 'Training a Multispecies DNA Language Model', 'Unsupervised Clustering of Genomic Regions'; SI Appendix Table S2

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things about a masked DNA language model. First, how well it predicts nucleotides it has not seen, measured as perplexity on a held-out chromosome, genome-wide and in non-repeat regions, and by position class (splice sites, start and stop codons, codon positions, intergenic and intronic) in a 1-Mb test region. Second, whether its embeddings, learned without labels, carry gene structure: a classifier trained on embeddings averaged over 100-bp windows must assign each window to a gene region class.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'Unsupervised Clustering of Genomic Regions' and 'DNA Motifs Revealed by High-Confidence Model Predictions'; Materials and Methods, 'Motif Analysis'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The model was trained on 8 RefSeq-annotated Brassicales reference genomes. Arabidopsis thaliana chromosome 4 was held out for validation and chromosome 5 for testing. Training windows of 512 bp were drawn with emphasis on exons, promoters and an equal amount of random windows. For the embedding task, gene annotation came from EnsemblPlants; intergenic windows fully covered by repeats form a separate Repeat class, and windows with ambiguous annotation were dropped.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, 'Pretraining' and 'Analysis of Model Embeddings'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Perplexity is the exponential of the cross-entropy loss; lower is better. Table S2 reports chromosome-wide and non-repeat test perplexity for three models that differ only in the loss weight on repeats. For gene regions, a scikit-learn logistic regression with inverse-frequency class weights and cross-validated L2 strength is trained on standardised window embeddings; each chromosome is predicted by a model trained on the others. The text reports per-class accuracy only for CDS (96%) and ncRNA (51%), and says k-mer frequency features do worse (SI Appendix, Figure S1).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results and Materials and Methods, 'Analysis of Model Embeddings'; SI Appendix Table S2

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: The A. thaliana reference genome, with chromosome 5 as test set, the 1-Mb region Chr5:3,500,000-4,500,000 for position-class perplexity, and genome-wide 100-bp windows annotated from EnsemblPlants for gene region classification. The paper gives no window or position counts; the 1-Mb region contains 264 genes and 471 transcripts.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results and Materials and Methods

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Chromosome hold-out. For perplexity, A. thaliana chromosome 4 is validation and chromosome 5 is test. For gene region classification, each chromosome is predicted by a classifier trained on the remaining chromosomes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, 'Pretraining' and 'Analysis of Model Embeddings'

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Perplexity (lower is better) for the sequence modelling tasks; per-class classification accuracy and a confusion matrix (higher accuracy is better) for gene region classification.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods; Figure 2B legend

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: GPN variants only: three repeat loss weights (1, 0.1 and 0) and a model trained on the A. thaliana genome alone, which had test perplexity 3.13 (3.17 on non-repeat regions). For gene regions, k-mer frequency features are the comparison (SI Appendix, Figure S1).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, 'Pretraining'; SI Appendix Table S2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Whole chromosomes are held out: chromosome 5 is never used in training, and the region classifier is evaluated leave-one-chromosome-out. The other seven training genomes are related species, and the paper does not discuss sequence shared between them and the test chromosome.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None reported for the perplexities or accuracies: single values, no seeds or intervals.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; SI Appendix Table S2

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A nucleotide position for perplexity; a 100-bp genomic window for gene region classification.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Arabidopsis thaliana for evaluation; the training set adds seven other Brassicales species.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'Training a Multispecies DNA Language Model'

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: No experimental assay: labels are the reference genome sequence itself and EnsemblPlants gene annotation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, 'Analysis of Model Embeddings'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only: 512-bp windows of unaligned genomic sequence with masked positions.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Perplexity is zero-shot from the pretrained model. Gene region classification is a linear probe: logistic regression on frozen, averaged embeddings.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'Unsupervised Clustering of Genomic Regions'

strengths.text: Test data are a whole held-out chromosome, and the region classifier is scored leave-one-chromosome-out, so test windows are not neighbours of training windows.
Perplexity is reported separately for non-repeat regions, so a reader can see the effect of repeats on the genome-wide figure.
The published model and the processed Arabidopsis data used by the study are on Hugging Face.

limitations.text: This is the authors' internal evaluation of their own models on one organism, Arabidopsis thaliana. No other DNA language model is scored, and there is no leaderboard.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results; SI Appendix Table S2

limitations.text: The text gives only two per-class accuracies (CDS 96%, ncRNA 51%); the full confusion matrix is a figure. The authors note that ncRNA annotation errors may explain some confusion.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'Unsupervised Clustering of Genomic Regions'

profile.summary: The MPRabc paper's evaluation of enhancer-gene link predictors on K562 cells. Predicted links are scored against a gold-standard set of 10 356 CRISPRi perturbations (471 positive, 9885 negative) using the benchmarking pipeline of Gschwind et al., with area under the precision-recall curve as the main metric. It is useful to regulatory genomics researchers comparing enhancer-gene models, but it is one paper's run on one cell line.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Methods, 'Benchmarking'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model can tell which candidate enhancers regulate which genes in K562 cells. The truth set is enhancer-gene pairs tested by CRISPR interference: a pair is positive when perturbing the enhancer significantly reduced the gene's expression. The paper uses the systematic benchmarking pipeline of Gschwind et al., which pools CRISPR perturbation results into a gold standard and asks how well model scores recover them.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Methods, 'ENCODE-rE2G' and 'Benchmarking'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Candidate enhancers are DNase-seq peaks called with MACS2, resized to 500 bp, keeping the top 150 000 by read count; every candidate within 5 000 000 bp of a gene's TSS forms a candidate pair. DNase-seq, H3K27ac ChIP-seq and Hi-C come from ENCODE. Models are evaluated on predefined CRISPRi datasets from Gschwind et al., and the paper reports the K562 set of 10 356 perturbations. MPRabc itself was trained on K562 CRISPRi-labelled pairs, as Gschwind et al. recommend.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, 'Dataset', 'ENCODE-rE2G' and 'Benchmarking'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Model scores are intersected with the labelled pairs and AUPRC is computed; precision at 70% recall is the secondary metric, using the pipeline's default operating point. Uncertainty comes from 10 000 bootstrap replicates of the labelled pairs, with 95% percentile intervals. The paper reports MPRabc at AUPRC 0.707 (95% CI 0.663 to 0.746), against the ABC model at 0.612 and ENCODE-rE2G at 0.634, and ablations that drop the MPRALegNet or Sei features.

profile.summary: The GPN paper's own test of unsupervised, genome-wide variant effect prediction in Arabidopsis thaliana. A variant score is checked by whether its most extreme tail is enriched for rare variants in the 1001 Genomes data and for GWAS hits in the AraGWAS Catalog, using Fisher's exact test, with phyloP and phastCons conservation scores as comparators. There is no labelled truth set and no train or test split: the endpoint is population genetic signal.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, 'Unsupervised Variant Effect Prediction'; Materials and Methods, 'Variant Effect Prediction'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a genome-wide variant score puts likely functional variants in its lowest tail. Three readouts are used: how variant consequence types rank under in silico mutagenesis of a 1-Mb region; enrichment of rare over common variants among the lowest-scoring 1001 Genomes SNPs; and enrichment of GWAS hits among the lowest-scoring AraGWAS variants. The paper scores variants with the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate to the reference allele.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'Unsupervised Variant Effect Prediction'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: In silico mutagenesis covers all possible SNPs in Chr5:3,500,000-4,500,000, annotated with Ensembl VEP; types with at least 1,000 variants are compared. The rare versus common set is over 10 million SNPs from the 1001 Genomes genotype matrix, where rare means allele count 1 and common means allele frequency above 5%. The GWAS set is AraGWAS summary statistics for 462 phenotypes (minimum allele count 6), with hits defined by the permutation-based threshold AraGWAS recommends, or by Bonferroni as a sensitivity check. The figure legend describes around half a million GWAS-tested variants.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, 'Variant Effect Prediction'; Figure 6 legend

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each score is thresholded at a quantile (varied from 0.1% to 10%) to call variants putatively functional, and the odds ratio and P-value come from Fisher's exact test. Rare versus common is reported at the lowest 0.1%; GWAS enrichment at the lowest 1%. For GWAS, scores are also combined with linkage disequilibrium (GPN x LD, a weighted sum over squared correlations within 100 kb), and the same transform is applied to phyloP and phastCons; the unweighted LD Score is a baseline. When comparing with phyloP and phastCons, variants those scores cannot cover are excluded. In silico mutagenesis ranks variant consequence types by the first percentile of their GPN scores; a side analysis compares the share of repeat variants below the first missense decile across models with repeat loss weights 0, 0.1 and 1.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Materials and Methods, 'Variant Effect Prediction'

profile.summary: A single-laboratory study that reclassified 121 BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants of uncertain significance (VUS) from 120 patients in two steps: first with the standard ACMG/AMP system, current SVI recommendations and new data, then with the ClinGen ENIGMA expert panel specifications on the same data. It reports how many VUS each step moved to benign or likely benign. It is relevant to clinical variant scientists choosing classification rules for BRCA1 and BRCA2, not to model comparison.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How far gene-specific expert panel rules change the classification of existing VUS compared with the general ACMG/AMP rules, when both are applied to the same up-to-date evidence. The endpoint is the share of VUS reclassified, and in which direction.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: 121 VUS (40 in BRCA1, 81 in BRCA2) classified between January 2018 and November 2023 were taken from the laboratory's internal database. These were reclassified in two steps (t2 and t3) from the original classification (t1). All reclassifications were done by one experienced variant analyst. Both steps used the Tavtigian point-based scoring system, but the ENIGMA rules require -2 points for likely benign.

The study counts VUS moved to likely benign or benign at each step: 20% (n = 24) at t2 and 83.5% at t3, with none moved to likely pathogenic or pathogenic. There is no external truth set; the authors attribute most of the difference to the ENIGMA BP1_STR code, applied to 93 variants.

profile.summary: The Jores et al. 2021 study measured the strength of tens of thousands of Arabidopsis, maize and sorghum core promoters with a STARR-seq reporter assay in tobacco leaves and maize protoplasts, then trained a linear model and a convolutional neural network to predict promoter strength from sequence, scored on a random 10% hold-out. It is a reference point for plant regulatory sequence models, for example when comparing a DNA model's promoter strength predictions in the two assay systems.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well a model predicts core promoter strength, the log2 enrichment of a promoter's reporter output relative to the 35S minimal promoter, from the promoter DNA sequence. profile.summary: A single-centre study that reclassified 450 BRCA1 missense variants with conflicting ClinVar interpretations (ClinVar accessed 20 December 2022) with two methods: the automated VarSome tool and manual curation under the CanVIG-UK BRCA1/BRCA2 gene-specific guidance. profile.summary: A study that combines two saturation genome editing (SGE) screens of the BRCA2 DNA binding domain into four composite functional models, checks each against known pathogenic and benign variants, and then feeds the best one (the Integrated VarCall model) into ClinGen BRCA1/2 expert panel classification rules. It reports sensitivity and specificity against ClinVar and HDR assay standards, and the share of 6383 variants that could be classified. It is relevant to clinical variant scientists using BRCA2 functional data.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things. First, how accurately each functional model (two original SGE studies, a concordance model, an Integrated VarCall model, an Integrated GMM model and a secondary concordance model) separates known pathogenic from benign variants. Second, how many BRCA2 variants can be classified as pathogenic or benign once the best functional model's evidence is added to the ClinGen rules.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: 6383 SNVs were scored in both SGE studies (HAP1 cells and humanised mouse ES cells); 1041 of them had discordant results. The Integrated VarCall model pools raw scores from both studies in a Bayesian hierarchical model with batch effects; silent variants are assumed benign and nonsense variants pathogenic, and the prior probability of pathogenicity is 0.2. Reference standards are 158 ClinVar P/LP and B/LB missense variants not influenced by SGE results and common to all six models, and 316 HDR assay missense standards.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Because all models reach close to 100% when every pathogenic or benign category is counted, the comparison uses only the Pathogenic_Strong and Benign_Strong/Moderate categories: sensitivity against P/LP standards (or HDR abnormal) and specificity against B/LB standards (or HDR normal). The Integrated VarCall model reaches 98.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity on the ClinVar standards, and 97% and 100% on the HDR standards. Its functional calls are then combined with other evidence under ENIGMA specification version 1.2.0 and the classification yield is counted. A separate case-control analysis tests whether Pathogenic_Strong missense variants raise cancer risk: odds ratios from logistic regression adjusted for age and ancestry, 5.46 (95% CI 4.07 to 7.48) for breast cancer and 6.83 (95% CI 4.51 to 10.40) for ovarian cancer, using Ambry Genetics cases and AllofUs controls.

profile.summary: A SEQC2 study that built a high-confidence set of somatic copy number gains, losses and loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH) regions for the hyper-diploid breast cancer cell line HCC1395, and used it to score six CNV callers on whole-genome and whole-exome tumour and normal sequencing under varied conditions. The truth set comes from agreement across 21 WGS replicates and six callers (five for LOH), checked against microarrays and Bionano. It is useful to cancer genomics groups choosing a CNV caller or validating a somatic CNV pipeline.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How reproducibly and accurately somatic CNV callers detect copy gain, copy loss and LOH in a cancer genome whose ploidy is not two (HCC1395 ploidy 2.85), and how sequencing centre, WGS versus WES, FFPE fixation, tumour purity, read coverage, DNA input and library protocol change the result.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: For gains and losses, six callers were run on 21 fresh tumour and matched normal WGS replicates from six sequencing centres, giving 126 call sets. LOH calls come from the five callers that report LOH (CNVkit, Control-FREEC, DRAGEN, FACETS, HATCHet), giving 105 call sets, with their own score cut-offs for the confidence levels. Overlapping calls were split into disjoint intervals and scored for reproducibility within centre, across centres and across callers, then given strong, medium, weak or neutral confidence. The benchmark keeps strong-evidence calls and medium or weak calls supported by at least two of three orthogonal technologies (Affymetrix CytoScan, Illumina BeadChip, Bionano); neutral calls are excluded. The paper reports 346 gain calls (1525.6 Mb), 33 loss calls (87.9 Mb) and 320 LOH calls (1490.4 Mb). The deposited BED file holds 307 gain intervals (1503.9 Mb, counted from the saved file) against the paper's 346; its 33 loss and 320 LOH rows match the paper.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A call set is scored by genomic overlap with the high-confidence set: precision is the fraction of called CNV regions that match, recall the fraction of high-confidence regions that are called, and F1 their harmonic mean, computed with BEDTools. Reproducibility between call sets uses the Jaccard index of region lengths. Chr6p, chr16q, chrX and gap regions are excluded. The authors state that only the qualitative class (gain, loss, LOH) is benchmark-grade; copy number values and breakpoints are not.

profile.summary: SAFFRON is a framework and an 8-task benchmark for asking whether embeddings from spatial transcriptomics foundation models (or single-cell models, or plain gene expression) capture known spatial variation. A sparse autoencoder is trained on a model's embeddings and its features are scored by their Spearman correlation with a known spatial measure, in six tissue-gradient tasks and two Alzheimer's plaque microenvironment tasks. It is aimed at researchers comparing spatial foundation model embeddings.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Benchmark; dataset card: introduction

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether any interpretable feature of a representation tracks a known measure of spatial variation tau. Global tasks use a 1-D spatial axis in a tissue (tumour-stroma, renal radial, cortical depth, crypt-villus, crypt-surface). Local tasks use three measures around amyloid-beta plaques in Alzheimer's model mouse brains: a DAM score, microglial density and distance to plaque.
sections.source_locator: Dataset card: introduction and Tasks

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Eight AnnData files on Hugging Face, each a processed subset of a public dataset: six global tasks (human colorectal tumour, mouse kidney, two human cortex sections, mouse ileum, human colon) and two local tasks (STARmap PLUS and MERFISH Alzheimer's model mouse brain). Each file holds expression, coordinates, tau, spatial domains or scoring masks, and two baselines: 50-component PCA and an SAE trained directly on gene expression.
sections.source_locator: Dataset card: introduction, Tasks and File contents

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A user passes a cell-by-feature matrix H (normally SAFFRON SAE features of the model's embeddings) to benchmark.score. For global tasks, benchmark.py computes, within each spatial domain with at least 10 scored cells, the maximum |Spearman rho| between any feature and tau, and returns the mean over domains. For local tasks it returns per-unit |rho| values: for DAM score and microglial density the single best feature over all pooled evaluated cells is chosen and its |rho| reported per sample (at least 20 cells); for distance to plaque the maximum over features is taken within each unit. No aggregate across the eight tasks is defined.
sections.source_locator: saffron/benchmark.py: global_score, local_scores

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository and install it with pip, load a task with benchmark.load (which downloads the file from Hugging Face), and score a feature matrix with benchmark.score. The README's example scores your model's SAE features and the stored PCA baseline.

profile.summary: BEND 2.0 tests whether genomic models can predict the effects of DNA changes and use those predictions to choose sequences, across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets: a sequence prior, splicing effects, cell-type contrasts, tissue identification, genetic background interactions and three design tasks. Seven tasks score linear readouts fitted to a model's frozen embeddings; the prior task needs nucleotide probabilities. It is aimed at developers and users of DNA language models and sequence-to-function models, with a maintained leaderboard.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; docs/tasks.md

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Five capabilities needed for DNA design: recovering a hidden base from context (prior); predicting how a mutation changes splicing (opensplice); accounting for cell type and tissue (context, tissue_identification); accounting for genetic background (background); and selecting edits or sequences that give a requested response (repair_percentile, cell_selective, atlas_profile).
sections.source_locator: docs/tasks.md: task table

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Tasks draw on OpenSplice (590,104 interventions in 466 genes), the Siraj saturation mutagenesis data (context, background, repair and cell-selective tasks), the atlas of AI-designed enhancers (7,657 sequences), GTEx v10 median expression (5,782 held-out genes, 51 tissues) and 512 GRCh38 windows for the prior. Holdouts follow biology: whole genes for OpenSplice, whole elements with their backgrounds for Siraj, separate source and candidate sequence families for Atlas, and distinct 1-Mb blocks for the prior. Data download from a fixed Hugging Face revision with checksums.
sections.source_locator: docs/tasks.md: Plan a run, What stays fixed; docs/data.md

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: For embedding tasks BEND fits a readout to frozen representations and scores it on the task's holdout; for variant effects the paper's readout is ridge regression on the change in embedding between variant and reference, with standardisation estimated on training data only; native prediction heads are scored separately. Each task has its own metric and direction, and the documentation says to compare scores within a task. Spearman-based tasks average per-gene or per-element correlations so each group has equal weight, and uncertainty comes from bootstrapping whole genes, elements or loci. Experimental references (one set of measurements predicting another) are reported for comparison but are not ceilings. Leaderboard submissions are rescored by the maintainers.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install the bend2 package with pip (Python 3.11 or later), try the included base-composition baseline on the Atlas task, then wrap your own encoder in a small my_model.py file that returns one embedding per sequence, run a task and view the results.

facts.value: OpenSplice (590,104 interventions, 466 genes); Siraj saturation mutagenesis (170,292 context substitutions in 128 elements, 68,026 paired mutations, 331 repair targets, 127 cell-selective loci); Atlas of AI-designed enhancers (7,657 sequences, 16 requests); GTEx v10 (5,782 held-out genes, 51 tissues); 512 GRCh38 prior windows. The paper also tests transfer of OpenSplice-trained predictors to 4,618 COMPASS mutations in 88 genes.

facts.value: Biological holdouts per task: five gene-held-out folds (OpenSplice); five element-held-out folds (Siraj context and background); separate source and candidate families (Atlas, 5,246 and 2,411); held-out genes (GTEx: 12,146 train, 1,350 validation, 5,782 test); distinct 1-Mb blocks (prior).

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Per task: conditional log loss in bits per base (lower better); macro-gene or macro-element Spearman (higher better); top-1 tissue accuracy (higher better); residual midrank percentile (lower better); cell-selective utility and gain over random selection in log2 (higher better). The leaderboard README also shows a combined score whose definition was not found in the saved files.

facts.value: The README results table lists AlphaGenome, NTv3 (100M and 650M, pre- and post-trained), Enformer, Evo2 20B, GENERATORv2, CENO 1B and DNABERT-2, with native outputs and fitted readouts, plus an experimental reference row. A base-composition baseline runs on CPU.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Holdouts keep whole genes, elements or sequence families together; the prior windows avoid blocks used in earlier prior panels, though the documentation notes this does not mean they were unseen in pretraining. Submitters must declare known overlap of training data with benchmark sequences or labels.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95% bootstrap intervals that resample whole genes, elements or loci; Atlas reports two replicate values, which the documentation says are descriptive, not a confidence interval.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: Varies by task: a DNA window (prior), a mutation or intervention (splicing, context, background), a gene (tissue identification), an element or locus design request (repair, cell-selective) and a sequence design request (Atlas).

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human: GRCh38 windows, human cell lines HepG2 and K562 (Siraj), GTEx human tissues, and human cell types (Atlas).

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Exon inclusion measurements for mutations (OpenSplice), saturation mutagenesis reporter assays in HepG2 and K562 (Siraj, with ENCODE count data), reporter activity of designed enhancers in 12 cell types (Atlas) and bulk RNA-seq median expression (GTEx).

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only. Seven tasks take one fixed-width embedding per sequence; prior takes four nucleotide probabilities. Tissue identification needs 131,072-base inputs. Native outputs may also be scored separately.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Frozen embeddings with linear readouts fitted by BEND; no fine-tuning of the model inside the benchmark. Native output heads are reported separately.

strengths.text: Holdouts follow biological units (genes, elements, sequence families, genomic blocks), and uncertainty is bootstrapped over the same units.
Design tasks score a model's choices against measured outcomes, not only prediction accuracy.
A pip package, fixed data revision with checksums, and a leaderboard where maintainers rescore submissions.

limitations.text: Four of the eight tasks use the Siraj data, which is CC BY-NC 4.0: no commercial use.
Scores use linear readouts on frozen embeddings, so they measure what a linear probe can extract, not a fine-tuned model; native heads are scored separately.
Pretraining overlap with benchmark sequences is self-declared; for the prior task the documentation says the windows may have been seen in pretraining.
Human data only, and tasks have different units, so the documentation advises comparing within a task; the README's combined score is not defined in the saved files.

profile.summary: LncBench is a collection of 15 RNA task datasets released with the LncRFM long non-coding RNA language model, each a Parquet file with sequence, label and split columns and its own training entry point in the LncRFM repository; two sets are test only. It is useful to developers of RNA language models who want ready-split datasets; there is no paper in the saved sources and no leaderboard.
profile.summary_source_locator: Zenodo description; README.md: Downstream learning

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well an RNA sequence model, fine-tuned or with a trained head, predicts per-task labels on 15 datasets named lnc_binary, RNAErnie-lncRNA, iLoc-lncRNA D1 and D2, lncATLAS-Localization, lncATLAS-RCI, Disease, Expression, POSTAR3-UPF1, mRNA-DMS, mRNA-Structure, 5UTR-MRL, RiNALMo-Splice, RNAChallenge and lncRNA-Structure. The README describes only some labels: Expression has five ordered categories, splice labels carry a donor or acceptor site and a value, DMS labels are per-base values and structure labels are base-pair index lists. The saved sources do not otherwise describe what each task measures.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Downstream learning; Zenodo file list

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each of the 15 files carries its own train, validation and test assignment in a split column, which the loader preserves. RNAChallenge and lncRNA-Structure hold test data only and are used with a trained task head. The Zenodo record says CC BY 4.0 covers the authors' own contributions and upstream data keep their original terms. The saved sources do not say where each dataset comes from or how its split was drawn.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo description; README.md: Downstream learning; lncbench_data.py

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each task has its own training script. The scripts select the best epoch on a validation metric (F1, micro-F1, ROC AUC, Pearson correlation or Pearson r squared, depending on the task) and then report final test metrics. No aggregate score across tasks and no leaderboard are described. The README lists comparison models (RNA-FM, structRFM, RNAErnie, SpliceBERT, UTR-LM, RiNALMo micro, LncRNA-BERT) without results.
sections.source_locator: LncDowntask scripts; README.md: Comparison methods

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Create the conda environment and install LncRFM, download the pretrained weights and the LncBench files from Zenodo, then run a task's training script with --data_file pointing at its Parquet file. The README's example trains a frozen-encoder adapter on iLoc-lncRNA_D1.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Not described in the saved sources.

facts.label: Entity type

facts.label: Organisms

strengths.text: Splits are fixed inside each file, and the loader preserves sample order and split membership, so results from different models use the same partitions.
Data are on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 for the authors' contributions, and the training code is MIT licensed.

limitations.text: No paper or task documentation was found: dataset origins, sizes, split construction and leakage controls are not described in the saved sources.
Upstream data keep their original terms, which the saved sources do not list, so reuse terms per dataset are unclear.
No leaderboard, reference results or aggregate score; the training scripts are written for the LncRFM model's backend and environment (Python 3.10, CUDA 11.8 state-space kernels).

profile.summary: ClinBench is a patient-level benchmark that Blank Bio assembled to evaluate checkpoints of its Ladon bulk RNA-seq foundation model: 142 survival, treatment-response and patient and tumour characteristic prediction tasks scored on frozen embeddings. It is described only in a section of the Ladon technical report, which uses it to relate pretraining loss to downstream performance. The task list, cohorts and splits are not published, so other groups cannot run it.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report pages 40 to 42: scaling section and Methods, 'Clinical benchmark'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether embeddings from an RNA-seq foundation model carry information about patient outcomes and characteristics: survival, treatment response and patient and tumour characteristics. In the report it is used to test whether lower pretraining reconstruction loss goes with better downstream performance.
sections.source_locator: Report page 40

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: 142 tasks: 85 within-cohort tasks, each scored by three-fold cross-validation repeated five times, and 57 cross-cohort survival tasks, where a model trained on the other cohorts of the same cancer type is tested on a held-out cohort; each held-out cohort counts as a separate task. The report does not list the tasks, cohorts, outcome definitions or patient counts.
sections.source_locator: Report page 42: Methods, 'Clinical benchmark'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each checkpoint's frozen embeddings feed elastic-net Cox models for survival and logistic regression for classification, with regularisation chosen by cross-validation on training data. Survival is scored by Harrell's concordance index and classification by AUROC, and the reported score is the unweighted mean over all 142 tasks. Four feature representations (raw, standardised, PCA 32, PCA 64) are tried per checkpoint and the one with the highest average score is reported. A gene-expression baseline uses the same tasks, splits and heads on log gene expression.
sections.source_locator: Report page 42: Methods, 'Clinical benchmark'

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 142 tasks: 85 within-cohort and 57 cross-cohort survival tasks. The cohorts, sample counts and outcome definitions are not given in the report.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Within-cohort tasks: three-fold cross-validation repeated five times. Cross-cohort tasks: train on the other cohorts of the same cancer type, test on the held-out cohort.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Harrell's concordance index for survival and AUROC for classification (higher is better for both); the summary is the unweighted mean over 142 tasks.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: A gene-expression baseline on log-transformed gene expression with the same tasks, splits and heads; the figure line uses PCA with 32 components.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Feature transformations are fitted on training samples only, and cross-cohort tasks hold out whole cohorts. The report does not say whether ClinBench samples were in Ladon's pretraining data.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None reported for ClinBench scores: Figures 20 and 21 show checkpoint points with no intervals in the text layer.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A patient's bulk RNA-seq sample with an outcome or characteristic label.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human patients (cancer cohorts, by the report's description of cross-cohort tasks within cancer types).

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Bulk RNA sequencing; labels are clinical outcomes (survival, treatment response) and patient and tumour characteristics.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Frozen embeddings of the RNA-seq profile, or log gene expression for the baseline.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Linear probe: elastic-net Cox or logistic regression on frozen embeddings; the foundation model is not fine-tuned.

strengths.text: Includes cross-cohort survival tasks that test transfer to a held-out cohort, not only cross-validation within one cohort.
The gene-expression baseline uses the same tasks, splits and prediction heads as the model, so the comparison is like for like.

limitations.text: The task list, cohorts, outcome definitions and splits are not published, so the benchmark cannot be rerun or checked.
The 142 tasks are not 142 independent cohorts: 85 are within-cohort cross-validation tasks, and each held-out cohort counts as its own task.
The best of four feature representations is reported per checkpoint, a choice made on the evaluation tasks themselves.
It is a vendor's internal benchmark for its own model, described in a report with no stated licence, and no ClinBench numbers are printed in the text layer.
